articles.content_orig:
Iran War Updates: U.S. and Iran hold first talks since June after Trump threatens regime with annihilation
What to know about the Iran war today:
- Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian addressed the U.N. General Assembly on Wednesday, saying Iranians are "the victims of terrorism" by the U.S. and Israel, and have "never ever been an aggressor."
- A commercial vessel was struck in an attack in the Strait of Hormuz on Wednesday, killing one crew member and necessitating the evacuation of more than 20 more sailors, according to the Omani navy.
- U.S. and Iranian officials met Tuesday while both countries were at the U.N. gathering, President Trump said, shortly after threatening in his address that he may "annihilate" the Islamic Republic if a deal isn't reached soon to end the nearly seven-month war.
8 suicide attempts by U.S. sailors assigned to USS Abraham Lincoln strike group during its record-long deployment, Navy letter says
There were eight suicide attempts by sailors assigned to the USS Abraham Lincoln carrier strike group since it began its record-long deployment about 10 months ago, according to a letter from Acting Navy Secretary Hung Cao that was obtained Wednesday by CBS News.
CNN was first to report on the letter. CBS News has reached out to the Navy for comment.
The deployment of the Lincoln and its approximately 5,000 crew members came under scrutiny after family members of the sailors and members of Congress raised questions last month about the conditions aboard the carrier and concerns about the mental health of its service members.
The Lincoln and its strike group were sent to the Middle East after the Iran war broke out. It has since left the region and is returning to its home base of San Diego.
The strike group includes the carrier air wing, strike group and destroyer squadron staff, escorting destroyers and all the embarked aviation squadrons.
The letter was in response to questions from Democratic Sen. Kirsten Gillibrand of New York about reported conditions on the ship.
In a statement provided to CBS News, Gillibrand said that while the Trump administration "can find endless taxpayer dollars for bombs, ballrooms, and billionaires, but cannot take care of our service members, is completely unacceptable."
U.S. blockade has redirected 115 commercial vessels, military says
The U.S. military blockade on the Strait of Hormuz has now redirected 115 commercial vessels entering or exiting Iranian ports, according to U.S. Central Command.
The total is an increase of five ships since Monday, when the military last provided an update.
The blockade has become a renewed topic of conflict as Iran and the U.S. renewed negotiations this week at the U.N. General Assembly. Representatives from the United States, including Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff, met with Iranian officials on Tuesday and apparently found some common ground, with President Trump saying the meetings went well.
However, on Wednesday, Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesperson Esmaeil Baqaei reiterated that no deal will be signed until the U.S. removes the blockade on the Strait of Hormuz.
White House responds to Iranian president's speech at U.N.
President Trump is "courageously" fighting against the Iranian regime, the White House said Tuesday in response to a question about Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian's speech at the U.N. General Assembly.
"The Iranian regime has murdered thousands of its own people, killed Americans overseas, executed acts of terrorism in the Strait of Hormuz, and launched indiscriminate attacks against its neighbors in the region," Anna Kelly, White House principal deputy press secretary, said in a statement. "The President is courageously ensuring that such an evil country never possesses a nuclear weapon, which will make the entire world safer and more stable."
Through a translator, Pezeshkian said Iran was a victim of Israel and the U.S., and the U.S. is using the Strait of Hormuz "to impose their aggression upon us."
Iran "will never bow our head or bend at the knee. Iran must be understood by Mr. Trump and those who seek to bully us that we are ready for dialog and diplomacy and negotiations without accepting the language of force," Pezeshkian said.
Canada imposes new sanctions on Iran officials, entities
The Canadian government announced new sanctions Wednesday against several senior Iranian officials and state-run entities "for their role in the Iranian regime's brutal repression of its population."
The sanctions target five senior Iranian security and government officials and five state-run entities, the foreign ministry said in a statement, without providing specifics.
"These individuals and entities have contributed to Iran's efforts to suppress dissent and restrict fundamental freedoms of Iran's population, including through digital surveillance, censorship, unlawful violence, arbitrary detention and intimidation," the ministry said.
A protest movement in Iran sparked in late December by grievances over high living costs rapidly evolved into widespread anti-government demonstrations that peaked on Jan. 8 and 9.
Iranian authorities reported more than 3,000 deaths from the unrest, attributing the violence to "terrorist acts" orchestrated by the United States and Israel. Rights groups based abroad put the toll higher and accused security forces of firing at demonstrators.
Massive protests also erupted in Iran in Sep. 2022 following the death in custody of Iranian Kurdish woman Mahsa Amini, who had been arrested for allegedly violating strict dress rules for women.
UAE sanctions local branches of Iran's Bank Melli
The UAE central bank said Wednesday that it had imposed sanctions on the Emirati branches of Iran's Bank Melli, accusing it of violating local laws on money laundering, terrorism and arms proliferation.
The bank said in a statement that "it has been decided to prohibit all branches of Bank Melli Iran operating in the UAE from conducting any financial transactions to and from Iran, including trade finance and fund transfers."
It cited "non-compliance with the regulations, laws and supervisory decisions in force in the UAE, including the requirements and obligations set out under the legislation related to combating money laundering, the financing of terrorism and proliferation financing."
The announcement comes against the backdrop of the Middle East war, which began with U.S.-Israeli strikes on Iran in late February, as well as Washington's more recent economic pressure campaign against the Islamic Republic.
As part of that stepped-up campaign, the U.S. announced new measures at the end of August targeting Iran's trading partners, and sanctioned the director of the Dubai branch of Bank Melli.
Last month, the United Arab Emirates announced the suspension of trade and financial exchanges with Tehran.
German foreign minister: "Iran must engage constructively" in negotiations
Germany's foreign minister, Johann Wadephul, offered a direct criticism of Iranian negotiations in a meeting with his counterpart, Abbas Araghchi, on Tuesday at the U.N. General Assembly.
"Iran must engage constructively in talks for a sustainable solution to end the conflict in the region & unconditionally open the Strait of Hormuz, ensuring free, safe and toll-free navigation for all," he said on social media.
Wadephul's comments came as Iran continues to take a hard line in negotiations, demanding the U.S. remove its blockade on the Strait of Hormuz, end the war on all fronts, release frozen or restricted assets and agree to the Oman-Iran negotiated passage through the strait, according to Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesperson Esmaeil Baqaei.
Araghchi has yet to comment on the meeting with Wadephul, though the government shared photo of the two meeting on the sidelines of the U.N. General Assembly.

articles.title_orig: Iran’s president hits out at ‘bully’ Trump in UN speech but signals willingness to talk
articles.title_zh: Iran’s president hits out at ‘bully’ Trump in UN speech but signals willingness to talk
articles.content_orig:
Iran’s president, Masoud Pezeshkian, turned the tables on Donald Trump, describing the US as the true bully and terrorist in the Middle East while insisting that Iran had always shown a commitment to the negotiating table.
In a defiant speech to the UN general assembly in New York, his first since the US and Israel launched an all-out war on Iran, Pezeshkian repeatedly vowed that Tehran would never bend the knee to the US.
But he balanced defiance with a willingness to talk, saying: “It must be understood by President Trump and those who seek to bully us that we are ready for dialogue and diplomacy and negotiations but without the language of force.”
On Tuesday, the US president had told the UN he was weighing whether to “annihilate” Iran, but went on to hail renewed talks between Tehran and Washington’s negotiators.
A surprise three-hour meeting between Iran’s foreign minister, Abbas Araghchi, and the US special envoy Steve Witkoff on the sidelines of the assembly the same day was regarded as constructive by both sides. It was the first such meeting since June, but did not stop the US delegation from walking out at the start of Pezeshkian’s speech.
The Iranian president did not go into any details about the talks, but conveyed the impression that he was focused on winning the support of Iran’s Arab neighbours for the proposals Tehran has drawn up for the future of the strait of Hormuz, the vital waterway that has been intermittently blockaded since the start of the war, causing global energy prices to soar.
He made it clear Iran could not tolerate the strait being used to transport arms that could then be used against it, a statement that suggests the Islamic republic will demand the right to inspect ships travelling through the strait in the future. Iran’s goal, he said, was to live independently.
Pezeshkian accused Washington of “terrorism” for assassinating the supreme leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei at the start of the war. He held up photographs of the dead leader and more than 150 schoolchildren killed in the opening days of the conflict, before insisting Tehran had never started a war.
“We have only defended ourselves. We are not terrorists,” he said. “Our innocent people have been the targets of cowardly attacks and aggressions imposed upon our country.”
He said Iran had the right to pursue a peaceful civil nuclear programme and it did not want to build nuclear weapons.
He repeatedly argued that the answer to regional security lay in agreement within the region and not with outsiders such as the US. Iran did not see its neighbours as security rivals, he said, but as partners in security. “In today’s world, those that are unable to defend themselves will be trampled upon,” he added.
Iran has repeatedly targeted US allies in the region since the start of the war.
Insisting Iran was the true victim of terrorism, Pezeshkian questioned why “Israel kills, yet Iran is subject to sanction”. He added: “They kill, we are sanctioned. Iran did not seek special treatment but wanted equal rights.”
Pezeshkian’s speech received domestic praise, but the hardline secretary of the supreme national security council, Mohsen Rezaei, refused to describe the talks with the Americans as negotiations. He said: “Mr Araghchi [Iran’s foreign minister] has announced Iran’s conditions, and until Iran’s conditions are implemented, the strait of Hormuz will not be opened nor will there be any negotiation.”
He warned Iran’s neighbours implementing a US-induced ban on Iranian travel: “If you stand alongside the United States, we will not stand by and watch.” He cautioned that should Iranian flights face bans through regional cooperation with Washington, “their airports will have no flights either”.
Pezeshkian’s attendance at the UN’s signature diplomatic event, in the heart of Manhattan, had been in doubt as it was unclear whether the US would issue a visa. Ultimately, Washington granted the permit but denied visas to several members of Pezeshkian’s entourage.
In Tehran, the foreign ministry spokesperson, Esmail Baghaei, confirmed talks had taken place between the two sides but appeared not to confirm any shift in the Iranian negotiating position.
He said: “The interaction that took place with the American side was through Qatari mediation. This interaction was aimed at conveying Iran’s conditions, including the end of the war in all its dimensions, the cessation of American aggressive actions, the naval siege, and the economic war, the release of Iranian assets and so on.”
Aware of the potential domestic backlash, he added that Iran’s conditions had been conveyed.
Iran set seven preconditions before returning to talks, and in a new development over the past 48 hours it said the strait of Hormuz could be reopened within seven days if those conditions were met.
It is likely that the US and the Gulf states would have to accept a navigational route for shipping in the strait of Hormuz that requires commercial shipping to enter through a sea lane mainly in Iranian waters and under Iranian rather than Omani control.
The fact that the talks lasted three hours suggests some progress was made. The US side is under pressure to leverage down oil prices and increase the availability of refined oil before the midterm elections in November. The latest published figures suggest the number of identifiable tankers making it through the strait is fewer than five a day.
The blockage in the strait is made worse by uncertainty surrounding the control by the Houthis – the Iran-backed Yemeni paramilitaries – of a second energy transport choke point, the Bab al-Mandab strait that leads from the Red Sea into the Indian Ocean.
There is little sign that Trump wants to relaunch a full-scale war with Iran, or indeed with the Houthis, as Republicans battle to turn the domestic political agenda away from a hugely unpopular conflict that Americans think they are losing.
Iran is under ever more intense pressure from sanctions, and a US naval blockade is making it nearly impossible for it to export oil, depriving the country of badly needed foreign currency. Iran’s civilian aircraft on Wednesday faced a potential worldwide grounding owing to the threat of US secondary sanctions on any entity that engaged with Iran’s civilian fleet.
Iranian officials negotiated frantically with neighbouring countries to try to maintain an air bridge, but it appears that Oman and Iraq have been forced to close their airspace to Iranian civilian planes.

articles.title_orig: Idaho officials solved a cold case that may have a connection to the infamous 1982 'Tylenol murders'
articles.title_zh: Idaho officials solved a cold case that may have a connection to the infamous 1982 'Tylenol murders'
articles.content_orig:
Idaho officials solved a cold case that may have a connection to the infamous 1982 ‘Tylenol murders’
BOISE — Idaho law enforcement believe a man found dead after poisoning himself in a Boise church 44 years ago could have a connection to the 1982 Tylenol killings, an unsolved string of homicides that roiled the nation and changed the way consumers open over-the-counter pill bottles to this day.
Ada County Sheriff’s Office Det. Tim Cooper in a news conference Wednesday identified Dr. Mathew Francis Betkouski, a Lockheed Martin organic chemist who worked on NASA-related projects, as the man who poisoned himself with cyanide in Sacred Heart Catholic Church in Boise, Idaho and was buried without a name. The case was reopened in 2019 because a church member had asked about its progress.
Known as the “Unknown Wanderer,” before his identification, Betkouski had a “documented fascination” with chemistry and explosives. Odd behavior increased after he sustained a brain injury in 1974 from falling off a tall fence, Cooper said. Though he was plagued with mental illness, Cooper said Betkouski was a “brilliant man” who struggled to connect with people.
Betkouski attempted to obtain capsules of some kind in the Las Cruces, New Mexico area in March of 1982. Police were called to the pharmacy and he was escorted home, Cooper said. They discovered he was taking unauthorized “material” from his lab at the White Sands Test Facility in New Mexico and later found cyanide in his room. It Coworkers said Betkouski would often discuss how cyanide could be used in “the perfect crime.”
Bekowski received months of outpatient and inpatient psychiatric treatment at the UCLA The Resnick Neuropsychiatric Hospital in Los Angeles, but when he returned to work in Florida, he was terminated partly because his behavior had not improved. He also made frequent calls to chemical supply and pharmaceutical companies in Pennsylvania in the weeks before the Tylenol homicides.
Betkouski eventually sold his car and other possessions at his home in Las Cruces, New Mexico, where he lived, and disappeared.
When the man known as the “Unknown Wanderer” was found dead in the pews of the church on Dec. 4, he had two items on his person that would lead to his identity: Two key rings full of keys and a wallet. One key was a house key that led to a street in Jacksonville, Florida, known as “Mills Court.” Property records of homes on that street led investigators to a man whose brother disappeared in 1982. That lead caused investigators to set sights on Betkouski. They compared the brother’s DNA with DNA found on the unidentified man’s wallet. They had the same father, detectives discovered.
Betkouski was part of a prominent Los Angeles family and a graduate of Loyola University in Los Angeles. He was granted a teaching internship at The University of Dayton in Ohio, newspaper records show. He and his ex-wife were engaged in April 1967. She also graduated from the University of Dayton, records show.
Cooper maintained that while they will not name Betkouski as a suspect in the Tylenol homicides, their goal is to “generate new leads” and ask people with knowledge of his whereabouts in 1982 to come forward.
“We sent all our information to the Chicago area. It’s really not our job to name him as a suspect,” Ada County Sheriff Matt Clifford said during the press conference Wednesday. “What we are looking for is … Do you have any information?”
The chaos and uncertainty began in the greater Chicago area in the fall of 1982, when 12-year-old Mary Kellerman died in the hospital after consuming Tylenol capsules. Six more people, all below the age of 35 and also living in the Chicago area, died the same way.
Investigators discovered the capsules were laced with a lethal dose of cyanide, leading to a widespread recall of Tylenol and immediate removal of the medication across shelves nationwide.
Johnson & Johnson determined whoever laced the capsules did so after Tylenol left its distribution centers, meaning the bottles must have been taken off store shelves, poisoned with cyanide and eventually placed back on the shelf. Some of these stores were more than 20 miles apart.
Investigators had some suspects throughout the years, but their prime suspect was always James Lewis, a man who was convicted for trying to extort the makers of Tylenol . Lewis wrote a letter around the time of the poisonings to Johnson & Johnson, saying the killings would stop if they wired $10 million to a Chicago bank account belonging to a travel agency.
Lewis admitted to writing the letter, but claimed it was only to embarrass the travel agency, where his wife used to work. Lewis despised the agency’s owner, whom he believed stiffed employees on their paychecks, the Chicago Tribune reported. Lewis also told investigators how one might hypothetically poison grocery shoppers with cyanide during interviews after the killings, but never admitted to doing it himself. He maintained his innocence until his death in 2023.
Though some FBI agents always believed Lewis was behind “the Tylenol Murders,” as the press dubbed the homicides , former U.S. Attorney Dan Webb maintained there was never enough evidence to formally charge him, according to the Chicago Tribune.
Back in the winter of 1982, two months had gone by without any answers to who had poisoned seven people in Illinois. And Idaho law enforcement’s unidentified and “Unknown Wanderer,” Betkouski, was already dead.
At the time, Betkouski was a well dressed and well-off man who had poisoned himself with cyanide while sitting in a pew at Sacred Heart Catholic Church on Dec. 4. He was there around the time of confession service, fueling speculation about a possible confession — but the priest who was there at that time never provided a statement to investigators about what the man said before his death.
“We have heard various things that may have been said or done in the church that day, and some are interesting,” Cooper said. “But in the end, we cannot independently verify what was or wasn’t said in the confessional on the day Betkouski died.”
The man had sandy, dyed hair, was wearing a green long-sleeve shirt, blue jeans, a belt with a metal buckle, a bolo tie, a Seiko watch and cowboy boots.
“He was carrying a wallet, no cards in it, but you could still see the sweat lines where the cards used to be,” Clifford said. “The man’s fingernails were finally filed. His hair had been dyed in style, possibly with a razor. His pants looked like they had never been worn, or just or had just been pressed.”
Two key rings with nearly 30 keys between them were found on his person. He also had an ink marker, a lighter, $1,900 in cash and a typewritten suicide note.
The note began with, “In the event of my death,” and instructed whoever found him to use the money enclosed for his funeral, the Idaho Press reported in 2021. The man wished to be cremated and instructed the rest of the money be donated to the church.
The note ended with, “God will see to your honesty in this.”
It was signed by “Wm. L. Toomey,” an alias. Investigators believed he came from New Mexico, California or Arizona based on his tanned complexion, according to the Doe Network, a center for unidentified persons. Police attempted to chase leads across the country, but none surfaced, the network’s website says. He was buried as an unidentified man in Eagle, Idaho’s Dry Creek Cemetery with a rock labeled “Toomey” for a headstone.
Across the country, however, grocery stores were in chaos. A quarter of a million bottles of Tylenol were recalled nationwide, according to newspaper archives. Other focus areas included capsules distributed east of the Mississippi River, in North Dakota, South Dakota and part of Wyoming. Illinois investigators quickly established a task force of 15 officers to pursue leads. articles.title_orig: Judge set to rule on Trump administration’s rationale for White House media ban
articles.title_zh: Judge set to rule on Trump administration’s rationale for White House media ban
articles.content_orig:
The trio of media outlets that President Donald Trump abruptly banned from accessing the White House were in court Wednesday to argue their expulsion was unconstitutional and should be blocked immediately.
U.S. District Judge Timothy Kelly did not immediately rule on the request after hearing arguments from an attorney for CNN, Politico and MS NOW and a lawyer for the Justice Department.
During the roughly 45-minute-long hearing, Kelly, a Trump appointee, appeared particularly focused on the “due process” — or lack thereof — that the journalists whose hard passes were revoked received.
He said due process requirements laid out by the judges in earlier cases involving press access, including the appeals court, were not followed in this case. “The government says those cases were wrongly decided,” Kelly said, but he has a “duty” to apply them in this case.
Lawyers for the media outlets said in a court filing Monday ahead of the hearing that the president’s “ban could not be a more direct assault on the First Amendment nor a more blatant violation of our most fundamental constitutional principles.”
“The ban is unconstitutional and should be immediately restrained,” they contended, citing legal precedent in the District of Columbia and U.S. Supreme Court.
Ted Boutrous, an attorney for the outlets, told Kelly he should look past the administration’s new arguments that the ban was motivated by national security concerns, and focus on what Trump has said about his decision.
“He is our lead witness here,” Boutrous said, pointing to Trump’s comments over the past several days that the outlets were too “negative.”
“He keeps proving our point,” Boutrous said.
Late Tuesday, the Justice Department defended the ban in a court filing, arguing that Trump had decided the outlets “failed to maintain basic minimum ‘standards of professionalism and decorum expected of those given access to the White House Complex, including’ by ‘publishing sensitive or classified information.’”
The outlets’ “access to the White House is a privilege — not a right,” DOJ attorney Michael Velchik told the judge at the hearing.
He pointed to letters the White House Press Office sent to the three outlets alleging their coverage involved “trafficking in verifiable falsehoods about national security and other issues, and publishing sensitive or classified information.” The letters also were filed in court.
The articles cited in the letters included reporting on the construction of the White House ballroom and its related military security complex, the status of munitions supplies being used in the Iran war, an alleged FBI leak investigation involving a journalist, and sanctions on Russia. Also cited was a Politico article about bad “vibes” at Republicans’ midterm convention.
In the letters, the administration gave the organizations a deadline of 5 p.m. Friday to “contest this initial decision” to bar them from the White House or the decision “will be final,” the filing said.
Boutrous told the judge the letters were an attempt to manufacture rationale for the policy. Trump’s directive shows the result has been prejudged, he said.
“All of a sudden this is a national security issue” — a topic Trump didn’t mention at all when he announced and spoke about the ban on Friday, Boutrous added.
He urged the judge to let his clients get back to work. “These are urgent matters. We are at war,” the lawyer said.
Boutrous added that of the four CNN stories the White House complained about in its unsigned letter, only one was by a reporter who covers the building and has a hard pass that was renewed months after the story published.
Kelly questioned the government’s arguments. “I don’t know how a letter that they got after their pass was revoked,” the judge said, “could provide them with the kind of standards they would have to conform their conduct to.”
He did not rule from the bench but said he’d take action “as soon as I can.”
Ahead of the court hearing, more than four dozen media outlets and groups filed a friend-of-the-court brief urging the judge to side with the banned outlets. NBCUniversal Media, the parent company of NBC News, was among the groups that took part in the brief.
The administration’s reason for the ban, the filing said, was “transparently viewpoint discriminatory.”
“The current ban — and any future bans — are intended to impair the critical work of news organizations covering the presidency if this Court does not immediately intervene,” the group wrote in the filing.
Kelly was nominated to the bench by Trump in his first term but ruled against him in a similar case back in 2018, when the White House pulled press credentials from then-CNN reporter Jim Acosta.
In a post on Truth Social on Monday, Trump said Kelly is a “great judge” for the media outlets, and suggested he believes he’ll rule against his administration. “[A]s usual, we’ll go for appeal,” he wrote, “because Fake News people and publications that only write negatively” should not be “allowed access to the most important Office anywhere in the World.”
Trump also criticized the judge as “totally disloyal” in a separate post late Tuesday.
The three news organizations have pointed to similar remarks by Trump as proof they’re victims of impermissible “viewpoint discrimination.”
Trump announced the outlets’ ban from the White House in a Truth Social post Friday and said it was “a result of their constant ‘reporting’ FAKE NEWS!”
“Other Fake News Media Outlets to follow,” he added.
Responding to questions from a reporter in the Oval Office a short time later, Trump referred to it as “the ban on the free press.” “Very simple ban. I don’t want them in my office. I don’t want them here,” he said.
He said the policy was in response to “cumulative stories over the last few years.”
“They purposely write negative news. And they do that because they want to try and diminish the Republicans and a Republican administration,” he said. “If they could straighten themselves out, I’d love it,” he added.
The outlets’ suit said Trump’s “words leave no doubt that banning Plaintiffs from the White House is retaliation for their protected newsgathering and speech — retaliation that is intended to cow them into changing their reporting and threaten other journalists lest they suffer the same fate. That is a paradigmatic First Amendment violation” and “flatly unconstitutional.”
The ban has already impacted news coverage, the suit says.
CNN is a member of the five-network rotation “for the primary television pool (also called the network pool) and absorbs 20% of the costs associated with such coverage,” the suit says.
The pool covers “events and locations where there is limited physical space for journalists,” their court papers say, and for “most of what the President does each day, the pool is the only source of independent reporting, video, and photographs available to the press and the public.”
“When CNN is the designated network pooler, CNN’s crew supplies the video and audio of the events involving the President and other White House officials to the other four networks and, through them and through pool distribution arrangements, to news organizations and the public. Among the recipients of the pool material are the more than 1,000 local affiliate television stations across the United States that receive the pool feed through CNN.”
NBC, ABC, CBS and Fox News are the other members of the rotation.
MS NOW is a rotating member of the secondary pool, while Politico is a member of the rotating print pool.
CNN had been scheduled to be the pool camera Monday, and the other networks in the TV network pool jointly declined to step in and replace its coverage. In video that day of a ribbon-cutting ceremony at the White House, Trump’s remarks were inaudible in the absence of pool microphones.

articles.title_orig: Exclusive | Federal Prosecutors Open Probe Into Jeffrey Epstein’s Executors
articles.title_zh: Exclusive | Federal Prosecutors Open Probe Into Jeffrey Epstein’s Executors
articles.content_orig:
Federal prosecutors in New York have opened an investigation into the two co-executors of the estate of convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein, The Wall Street Journal reported Wednesday.
No charges have been filed against the co-executors, Epstein's longtime lawyer Darren Indyke and accountant Richard Kahn.
The Journal said that in recent months, prosecutors in the U.S. attorney's office for the Southern District of New York have scheduled interviews with potential witnesses and requested documents about those witnesses' dealings with Indyke and Kahn.
The Journal also cited a report it published last year saying the two men "were officers of Epstein entities that obscured transactions, arranged cash for Epstein, made payments to women and facilitated Epstein's immigration schemes."
Indyke and Kahn have denied wrongdoing.
The Journal, citing documents, reported that Indyke could receive $50 million and Kahn could get $25 million from Epstein's estate because they are beneficiaries of a trust that will collect Epstein's remaining assets after claims against the estate are settled.
CNBC has requested comment from a spokesman for the U.S. attorney's office and from Indyke and Kahn about the Journal's report.
Epstein, 66, killed himself in a federal jail in Manhattan in August 2019, weeks after he was arrested on child sex trafficking charges.
Epstein's estate in February agreed to pay out as much as $35 million to settle a class action lawsuit in U.S. District Court in Manhattan that had accused Indyke and Kahn of aiding and abetting Epstein's sex trafficking of young women and teenage girls.
The proposed settlement does not include any admission of misconduct by either Indyke or Kahn. The judge handling the case on Sept. 18 endorsed a proposal by the suit's plaintiff to notify potential class members to submit claims on the settlement by conducting a four-week-long social media campaign on Facebook and Instagram.
The estate earlier established a restitution fund for Epstein victims that paid out $121 million to more than 130 women and has paid or committed to pay $48 million to nearly 60 additional women in separate settlements.
Lauren Hersh, CEO of World Without Exploitation, an advocacy group for Epstein survivors, in a statement Wednesday said, "We welcome the news that federal prosecutors are investigating Darren Indyke and Richard Kahn and asking questions that should have been asked years ago."
"Survivors deserve a full accounting of how Epstein and those in his orbit were able to operate for so long, and accountability for everyone who enabled or participated in their exploitation," Hersh said.
New Mexico Attorney General Raúl Torrez, whose office is conducting its own investigation into Epstein, said in a statement that he was aware of the Journal's report. Epstein maintained a residence in New Mexico.
"While we cannot comment on any potential federal investigation, this reporting only underscores the importance of full transparency and cooperation among all agencies charged with pursuing accountability," Torrez said.
"Our office has repeatedly sought access to the complete, unredacted records that may be relevant to New Mexico's ongoing work. We hope that federal authorities will now be willing to share any pertinent information without further delay," the attorney general said. "Survivors and the public deserve answers, and no institution should withhold information that could help advance justice."
Kahn and Indyke earlier this year testified behind closed doors to the House Oversight and Government Reform Committee, which has been investigating Epstein and his connections to various individuals.
"Both Mr. Indyke and Mr. Kahn reject as categorically false the suggestion that they knowingly facilitated or assisted Mr. Epstein in his sexual abuse or trafficking of women, or that they were aware of that abuse while they provided professional services for him," Daniel Weiner, an attorney for Epstein's estate, told MS NOW in a statement in March.
Rep. Robert Garcia of California, the ranking Democrat on the House oversight panel, said in a statement after Kahn testified in March, "Jeffrey Epstein's massive sex trafficking ring would not have been possible without the consistent payments and services of his long-time accountant Richard Kahn."
"It's not credible that he had no knowledge of Epstein's activities, and his testimony today only raises more questions," Garcia said.

articles.title_orig: Stock Market Today: Dow, Nasdaq Slip; 10-Year Treasury Hits 19-Year High — Live Updates
articles.title_zh: Stock Market Today: Dow, Nasdaq Slip; 10-Year Treasury Hits 19-Year High — Live Updates
articles.content_orig:
Soaring Treasury yields aren't just bad for the government and its $40 trillion debt. They also threaten to raise borrowing costs, hitting everyone from homeowners to credit card users, while providing limited relief to savers and potential benefits to banks.
Government debt costs leaped higher Wednesday, the product of multiple factors including a fresh report showing higher inflation pressures, surging expectations for a Federal Reserve rate hike in October, and an auction for 5-year notes showing that Treasury demand was weak. Competition from hyperscaler debt issuance also is seen as an aggravating factor.
Yields responded by jumping more than they have in nearly a year and a half, dating back to April 2025 when President Donald Trump first announced so-called reciprocal tariffs against U.S. trading partners. Recent market liquidity efforts pushed by Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent have had no impact so far, with rates surging higher despite intensified buyback efforts on longer-dated debt.
The 10-year note, a benchmark for mortgages and other longer-term borrowing, saw its yield hit, 5.125%, a level not seen since prior to the global financial crisis. Similarly, the 2-year note, which typically responds to Fed rate expectations and signals rates for home equity, auto loans and other debt, climbed more than 13 basis points past 4.9% as traders priced in a strong possibility that the central bank would follow its hike last week with another in October.
One basis point equals 0.01% and yields move opposite prices.
Such moves generally portend higher borrowing rates that hit the U.S. economy where it hurts the most — consumers, who drive nearly 70% of all economic activity and hold nearly $19 trillion in total debt.
While savers will benefit with incrementally higher rates on their bank savings accounts, it's unlikely to offset the pain they'll feel elsewhere, said Dan North, senior economist with Allianz Trade North America.
"The consumer's the most important part of the economy," North said. "They're going from little tiny yields on savings to ever slightly bigger tiny yields on savings. So I don't think that really yet helps the consumer that much. But it sure does crush housing, and it [impacts] on all those personal consumer loans, the credit cards and so forth."
Indeed, the interest rate on plain-vanilla savings accounts is around 0.37% and has been on a modest decline since the Fed enacted three quarter-point cuts late in 2025, according to FDIC data.
Mortgage rates, though, have been on an entirely different trajectory and are likely to continue rising. A typical 30-year mortgage is now at 7.26%, up more than a quarter percentage point in just the past couple weeks and nearly a full point over the past year, according to Mortgage News Daily.
Credit card interest rates have been fairly steady over the past few years, but also are unlikely to stay that way if current trends hold up.
When the Fed hikes, it feeds directly into the prime rate, which is used as a baseline for adjustable-rate credit and most recently was at 7%, after rising a quarter point off last week's Fed move.
Taken together, the factors make it more expensive for consumers to borrow and less likely that they'll seek the loans and credit that fuel a lot of the activity in the $32 trillion U.S. economy.
"You raise the fed funds rate, rates in the short term and effectively all along the curve go up," North said. "If it makes it harder for somebody to buy a car, then there's less demand for cars and there's less demand for auto workers, and the economy slows down. That's sort of basic economics, but that's how it works."
There are some positives from the higher rates.
Aside from whatever benefit savers get, banks can benefit. The industry's model is based on a variety of factors that can benefit in times of higher rates, from what they can charge borrowers to the margin they earn from what they charge to what they pay depositors, as well as the opportunity to get better return on their cash.
However, even bank stocks were mostly lower Wednesday as dramatically higher yields could slow loan demand and broader economic activity, which otherwise has been solid. The Atlanta Fed is tracking GDP growth of 5.1% for the third quarter, another element that could be factoring into higher yields.
Persistently higher yields, though, pose dangers to that growth picture.
"Smaller and medium enterprises are going to be suffering the worst because they have less ability to borrow," North said. "Less availability of credit makes it more difficult."

articles.title_orig: Death of Presley Gerber, Cindy Crawford's son, sparks questions over drug supplier, L.A. luxury rehab center
articles.title_zh: Death of Presley Gerber, Cindy Crawford's son, sparks questions over drug supplier, L.A. luxury rehab center
articles.content_orig:
Death of Presley Gerber, Cindy Crawford’s son, sparks questions over drug supplier, L.A. luxury rehab center
-    Click here to listen to this article
See more from the L.A. Times in Google Search. Set us as preferred
Detectives are trying to trace the supplier of the drugs that Cindy Crawford’s son, Persley Gerber, fatally overdosed on in Santa Monica rehab last weekend, according to law enforcement sources.
Gerber, 27, died at a luxury rehab center in Santa Monica on Sunday.
The Santa Monica Police Department said there is no indication of foul play at this time and that they are also investigating Gerber’s apparent overdose.
The sources told The Times the investigation is in its early stages.
The Los Angeles County Medical Examiner’s office conducted an autopsy Monday but deferred a cause and manner of death pending toxicology results for substances in Gerber’s system and that is expected to take several weeks, if not months, according to the office.
Gerber had entered the Resolution Living facility in Santa Monica just hours before his death, police said.
According to Resolution Living’s website, the house is a “Mental Health Recovery Residence.” The website describes it as part of a program that includes partial hospitalization and intensive outpatient treatment for a myriad of mental health issues, including depression, trauma and addiction, and offers dual diagnosis treatment for co-occurring disorders.
Santa Monica police received a call reporting a cardiac arrest and another call for an overdose at the center. Officers arrived at Resolutions Living, a $7.7-million, seven-bedroom mansion, at about 9:35 a.m. Sunday, a law enforcement source told The Times.
Resolutions Living did not return calls seeking comment.
It has become fairly common for police to now attempt to trace back the supplier of drugs in an overdose case.
Officials confirmed this week that Hayden Panettiere died from the toxic effects of fentanyl and other drugs, including a generic version of Xanax. Federal authorities probing her death are focusing their investigation in Los Angeles and are looking into whether the actor procured nonprescription pills from an area dealer. Drug Enforcement Administration agents and local investigators have questioned several people about the circumstances of her Aug. 16 death and have focused on her taking what was described as counterfeit pills before her demise.
The death of “Friends” star Matthew Perry sparked a sprawling drug investigation. Five people were charged with conspiracy to distribute ketamine to Perry, who died from acute effects of the drug.
Little is known about the Santa Monica police probe into Gerber’s death.
L.A. attorney Brian Claypool, who handles wrongful death litigation, said the autopsy and toxicology results “will be crucial in this tragic death to ascertain legal liability.”
Attorney Glen Jonas said depending on what police find, the rehab center could face scrutiny. Both attorneys said it is likely police will look closely at staffing, how the emergency was handled and other issues.
There have been cases in the past where drugs have been delivered into rehab centers.
The family of a Riverside woman sued a sober living center after she was found dead of a drug overdose.
In 2022, Edwin Oliva, of Montebello, was sentenced to over 33 years in federal prison for providing a lethal dose of fentanyl. During the early hours of Feb. 28, 2019, Oliva gave a woman a line of drugs to snort and did not tell her the substance was fentanyl — a powerful synthetic opioid. Believing the substance to be cocaine, the victim ingested the drug, which resulted in a fatal overdose.

articles.title_orig: Trump rolls out the red carpet for Chinese President Xi Jinping despite U.S.-China tensions
articles.title_zh: Trump rolls out the red carpet for Chinese President Xi Jinping despite U.S.-China tensions
articles.content_orig:
Trump rolls out the red carpet for Chinese President Xi Jinping despite U.S.-China tensions
Washington — President Trump is offering a warm welcome to Chinese President Xi Jinping this week as the U.S. tries to choke China's supply of semiconductor chips for artificial intelligence advancement, as the two countries determine whether their fragile truce on tariffs will continue, and as concerns mount about China's relationships with Iran and Russia.
Xi's visit to the White House, the first in more than a decade, features a state arrival ceremony Wednesday, with Mr. Trump taking part along with U.S. military personnel.
Thursday will bring a formal meeting of the two presidents and a state dinner. Xi's wife, Peng Liyuan, is joining the trip.
Mr. Trump and Xi last met in May, when Xi welcomed the U.S. president for a state visit in Beijing.
What to expect on the schedule
Mr. Trump welcomed Xi and his wife at Joint Base Andrews late Wednesday, a rare instance of a sitting president greeting a foreign leader on the tarmac instead of awaiting them at the White House.
A military band played as Xi and his wife exited a massive Air China jet while the American president and first lady awaited them on a red carpet at the bottom of the stairs. The arrival ceremony, which included a flyover with two B-1 bombers, was quick, and Mr. Trump and the first lady departed about 10 minutes later.
On Thursday morning, the president and first lady Melania Trump will host another arrival ceremony for Xi and his wife on the White House South Lawn. The White House says the ceremony will feature nearly 500 service members from all branches of the U.S. military.
The U.S. and Chinese flags will be displayed on the South Portico, according to the White House. The U.S. Marine Band will play the anthems of both the U.S. and China, the White House says. Then, both Mr. Trump and Xi are expected to speak.
The arrival ceremony is also expected to have a military flyover with a B-2 Spirit bomber and four F-22s.
The presidents' spouses are expected to visit the Smithsonian National Museum of Asian Art on Thursday while Mr. Trump and Xi meet. A state dinner will be Thursday evening.
On Friday, the couples will have tea at the White House before heading to the National Archives. The visit will then conclude.
China experts say not to expect many big policy achievements
China experts say to not expect many tangible policy outcomes from the meeting. James Lewis, a distinguished fellow with the Tech Policy Program at the Center for European Policy Analysis, said there "isn't much of a formal agenda" for the two leaders.
"I'm not anticipating very much — I don't think anyone is," Lewis said. "Because this is largely for show. And it's largely a discussion between two very cautious and two very suspicious leaders."
"I don't think there's too much hope for policy achievements," said Jake Werner, director of the East Asia Program at the Quincy Institute for Responsible Statecraft.
"Probably more than anything, Trump loves a show," Werner added. "He loves to put on a show. And secondarily, he thinks he has a relationship with Xi Jinping, who he thinks is a big, strong man, and he values those sorts of relationships. And then I think … he has a desire to make sure that China doesn't use the power that it demonstrated that it has last year when it cut the U.S. off of rare-earth elements, and American factories started shutting down."
Mr. Trump has often praised Xi and cast his warm personal relationship with the Chinese leader as an asset. During his visit to Beijing earlier this year, Mr. Trump called Xi a "great leader" and said the two men have always been able to work out their disagreements.
As for the disagreements that could dominate this week's visit: This is the meeting of the three "Ts," as Lewis put it — trade, tech and Taiwan.
What Trump and Xi may discuss on tariffs and trade
On trade, the U.S. and China will have to decide whether to extend a truce on tariffs that expires on Nov. 10.
That deal, struck in Busan, South Korea, in October, lowered tariffs levied by both countries and paused restrictions on Chinese exports of rare earth minerals. It also said China would continue to buy large quantities of U.S. soybeans, a pledge China has failed to keep.
The truce allowed the two countries to climb down from a tit-for-tat trade war that sent U.S. and Chinese tariffs to more than 100% at one point in spring 2025.
Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, who met with Chinese Vice Premier He Lifeng over the weekend, said the Chinese have proposed a "bigger deal" on trade between the U.S. and China, beyond the trade truce brokered in Busan, South Korea, in October.
Bessent said Mr. Trump and Xi may meet "up to four times" this year, so they're open to different approaches. Thursday will be their second meeting.
"We're open to the idea of just continuing the Busan arrangement, or examining the bigger deal," Bessent told reporters Wednesday. "We're fine with both, and we're going to do what's best for the American people."
On Fox News Monday, U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said there will be an announcement establishing a U.S.-China "Board of Trade," which will determine a "relatively small subset of goods" that the two countries agree they should protect from trade disputes. That may include things like low-tech consumer goods and some agricultural products, Greer said. The idea of such a board was discussed when Mr. Trump and Xi met in May.
Trump and Xi may discuss artificial intelligence
Amid growing public pressure for the U.S. government to implement more safeguards around advanced artificial intelligence, Bessent shared over the weekend that the U.S. has proposed a new "notification system" alerting AI incidents that affect national security. He made the announcement following a meeting with Chinese Vice Premier He Lifeng.
"We want a shared vision of common goals and common threats," Bessent said, according to the Associated Press. "We think that just like any cross-border activity, that moving from opaque to more transparency between the No. 1 and the No. 2 AI powers in the world is very important."
It's not yet clear if Mr. Trump is on board with that idea. His most-voiced concern about AI is the need for the U.S. to beat China, and he has spoken out against the idea of reining in the speed of AI research. He slowed and altered an executive order allowing the government to voluntarily review the latest frontier AI models before they are released.
Lewis said Xi wants access to advanced computer chips and to be able to sell memory chips to the U.S. Nvidia, one of the leading designers of the chips that power AI models, is currently prohibited from selling its most advanced products in China, though Mr. Trump has allowed it to sell its H200 chips to "approved customers."
There is also growing concern that Chinese AI developers are using a method called "distillation" to train Chinese AI models based on U.S. frontier models, according to the federal government's Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency.
AI is on the Trump-Xi agenda, a White House official told reporters on a call Friday on the condition of anonymity, although the person didn't elaborate. A reporter asked the White House official if the president will have a substantive call with Xi about AI safety, and if Mr. Trump is prepared to extend or renew the existing semiconductor chip-related licenses with China.
"Those are both on the agenda, both AI and the current 'Busan' truce, and we'll know more once the two leaders meet," the White House official said.
Taiwan is a key issue for Xi
Beijing is looking to reclaim Taiwan and wants the U.S. to stay out of the way, Lewis said. The U.S. has a multibillion-dollar deal to sell arms to Taiwan, and "the Chinese hate that," Lewis said.

articles.title_zh: Trump officials weigh rolling back beef import plan as GOP midterm panic spreads
articles.content_orig:
Former Ag Sec. Criticizes Beef Imports
Johanns: Beef Imports Send Wrong Message, Hurting Ranchers Just as Profits Return
KANSAS CITY, Mo. (DTN) -- Mike Johanns, a former Republican Agriculture secretary, said Monday the Trump administration's move to increase beef imports is hurting cattle producers who had finally begun recovering after years of weak returns.
Johanns, a former Nebraska governor and U.S. senator who served as agriculture secretary under President George W. Bush, spoke at the start of an Ag Outlook Forum in downtown Kansas City.
Without directly mentioning President Donald Trump, Johanns criticized the federal government's intervention into beef markets. He described the issue as "white hot" in cattle country. Now that ranchers are benefiting from the stronger side of the cattle cycle, Johanns said the federal government should not intervene simply because beef prices are high.
"If you would take the last 20 years in the cattle industry, 10 of those years I lost money, maybe 12," Johanns said. "A handful of those years were probably break-even at best."
He added, "Finally, they're making some money, and the government steps in, and I just don't agree with that."
Citing high beef prices, Trump last month announced plans to allow 300,000 metric tons (661.4 million pounds) of imported lean beef to enter the country tariff-free over three months. The resulting ground beef would then be sold at a discounted price. Major farm groups immediately called for Trump to reverse course on the plan, but there has been no official word on changes. Responding to industry criticism, USDA rolled out new plans to promote heifer retention, expand local processing and strengthen U.S.-origin beef labels.
Johanns estimated the resulting decline in cattle values cost the average producer somewhere between $250 and $500 per head.
Returns have improved over the past couple of years, particularly for ranchers and cow-calf operators, Johanns said. That optimism was shaken by the administration's announcement that it would increase beef imports in an effort to lower beef prices for consumers.

"Finally, they're kind of healing the pain and seeing some opportunity going forward," he said. "Maybe we can expand the ranch. Maybe we can expand the herd. Then all of a sudden, there's this announcement out of Washington, and they're going, 'Whoa, wait a second! Where did that come from?'"
Producers who previously lacked the cash to make improvements were beginning to do so, he said. Others could consider buying a neighboring ranch if it became available. Johanns said those stronger returns reflected the traditional cattle cycle after years when ranchers frequently struggled to make money.
"Who steps up and says, 'Well, I think they're making too much money?' Our government," Johanns said.
He said producers were largely left to absorb the losses when cattle markets were weak.
"I hated it when the ranchers were losing money, but most of the time, they were," Johanns said. "They just had friendly bankers. That's the only way they could survive."
Ranchers' reaction goes beyond frustration over a short-term decline in cattle prices, the former secretary said. Stronger cattle prices had reached the point where producers repair their finances and consider investments that had been difficult to make during leaner years.
Johanns also questioned whether increasing imported beef would save consumers enough money to justify the financial impact on cattle producers. He said it would only have a modest impact, "maybe a few cents or something on a hamburger," but added that the detriment to cattle producers outweighs the consumer benefit.
The former secretary also touched on his own decisions to oversee beef imports and exports during his time at USDA. One of his biggest challenges when he became Agriculture secretary in 2005 was reopening foreign markets that had closed to U.S. beef following the discovery of bovine spongiform encephalopathy, or BSE, in Washington state in late 2003.
Johanns said that as he pressed countries such as Japan to reopen their markets to U.S. beef, foreign officials challenged the United States over restrictions it had placed on cattle and beef from other countries, including Canada.
"If you want others to buy our beef, what's your policy going to be on the other end of it?" Johanns said.
Reopening the U.S. market to Canadian cattle was controversial at the time, he noted, with cattlemen's organizations divided over the move. Johanns, however, drew a distinction between imports needed as part of a reciprocal trading system and importing more beef specifically to drive down domestic prices.
"To bring in beef to discount it -- like there's something wrong with our beef here -- that's not set well," Johanns said. "I don't think this is a giant revelation for anybody anywhere in the ag industry, but it is the reality of what's going on out there. There's just some really hard feelings."

articles.title_orig: Giants QB Jaxson Dart will have knee surgery, ending his 2026 season
articles.title_zh: Giants QB Jaxson Dart will have knee surgery, ending his 2026 season
articles.content_orig:
Jaxson Dart's season is over.
The New York Giatns quarterback will undergo surgery and land on injured reserve after getting hurt during Monday night's 28-6 loss to the Los Angeles Rams, head coach John Harbaugh announced. While Dart is expected to make a full recovery, his 2026 season will be over.
According to ESPN's Adam Schefter, Dart's injury includes damage to his left MCL, PCL and meniscus. There is reportedly no ACL damage.
Harbaugh met with reporters on Tuesday afternoon and said that Dart was continuing to be evaluated and they had not made any decisions on the quarterback's status. The team "learned a lot more" about the injury following the MRI.
Harbaugh confirmed the injury on Wednesday afternoon. He did stop short of ruling Dart out for the postseason, should the Giants make the playoffs, but Dart will have surgery in the near future.
Dart suffered the injury in the first quarter on Monday night and did not return to the game. X-rays were negative and the second-year signal-caller underwent an MRI on Tuesday after the team returned home from Los Angeles.
During the game's opening drive, Dart dropped back to pass and jumped to make a throw downfield while under pressure. He was sandwiched between Rams linebackers Josaiah Stewart and Byron Young before falling to the ground holding his left knee.
Jaxson Dart is down on the field after this play. pic.twitter.com/R059M6kM6e
— TSN (@TSN_Sports) September 22, 2026
After being tended to on the field, Dart limped off and was taken for further evaluation. He was initially listed as questionable to return before being ruled out. He returned later without his uniform and watched the remainder of the game from the sideline.
Jameis Winston, who signed a two-year, $13-million extension before Week 1, finished the game going 11-for-27 with 111 passing yards, an interception and taking two sacks. Now, with Dart out for the year, Winston will presumably take the reins the rest of the way.
Jaxson Dart among Giants' MNF injury concerns
Dart wasn't the only injured Giant coming out of Monday night.
Wide receiver Malik Nabers injured his right shoulder in the first quarter. Nabers told reporters afterward that the shoulder popped out and he popped it back in, allowing him to return to the game the next series.
Linebacker Brian Burns had his left ankle rolled on by a Rams offensive lineman and needed help getting off the field. He limped his way to the Giants' locker room and was diagnosed with a low ankle sprain. He reportedly wore a boot on his left foot and while he said it's "nothing serious," it's unclear if Burns will miss any time.
Left tackle Andrew Thomas suffered a groin injury on the team's final offensive play, but no update has been provided on his status.
The Giants entered the game without cornerbacks Deonte Banks and Paulson Adebo, who were ruled out due to injury.
The Giants' next two games are at home against the Tennessee Titans and Arizona Cardinals. They will go back on the road for Week 5 to face the Washington Commanders and return home for Week 6 against the New Orleans Saints. They will then travel to take on the Houston Texans before their bye in Week 8.

articles.title_orig: Microsoft refreshes its smaller Surface Pro and Laptop with Qualcomm’s X2 Plus
articles.title_zh: Microsoft refreshes its smaller Surface Pro and Laptop with Qualcomm’s X2 Plus
articles.content_orig:
Microsoft is refreshing its Surface Pro 12-inch and Surface Laptop 13-inch devices with Qualcomm’s latest Snapdragon X2 Plus chips. The smaller Surface devices retain the same design and hardware features from last year, with faster and more capable chips inside and higher price tags (thanks RAMageddon!).
Microsoft refreshes its smaller Surface Pro and Laptop with Qualcomm’s X2 Plus
The Surface Pro 12-inch and Surface Laptop 13-inch both have better battery life and performance, but higher price tags.
While the 12-inch Surface Pro started at $799.99 last year, it’s debuting on October 13th at a starting price of $1,149.99. Likewise, the 13-inch Surface Laptop was originally priced at $899.99, but it’s up to $1,199.99 this time around. There’s no base 8GB model this time, causing some of the price increase, as both devices launch with a minimum of 16GB of RAM and can be configured up to 24GB.
Pricing aside, Microsoft is promising that the six-core Snapdragon X2 Plus chips will deliver up to 18 percent more efficient battery performance, more than 60 percent faster graphics performance, and up to 95 percent faster local AI inferencing on the built-in NPU.
That’s a lot of percentages, but what it equates to on these devices is better battery life and improved performance. On the Surface Pro 12-inch Second Edition, as Microsoft calls it, that means an extra hour of web browsing (up to 13 hours in total), and on the Surface Laptop 13-inch Second Edition it’s two extra hours of web browsing usage (up to 18 hours in total).
Microsoft is using similar displays on these models as last year, so the Surface Pro 12-inch has a 2196 x 1464 (220 PPI) LCD display that runs at up to 90Hz. The Surface Laptop 13-inch still ships with a 1920 x 1280 (178 PPI) display that only runs at 60Hz. Both displays have been upgraded from 400 nits of brightness to 500 nits, though.
Port selection remains the same, too. Both devices include two USB-C 3.2 ports, and the Surface Laptop 13-inch also has a USB-A 3.2 port and a 3.5mm headphone jack. Both also support Wi-Fi 7 and Bluetooth 5.4 connectivity.
I’m surprised that Microsoft hasn’t upgraded at least one of these smaller Surface devices with a haptic trackpad, particularly because Windows 11 now adds subtle haptic nudges, and the Surface Laptop Ultra ships with haptic feedback. Microsoft is launching a second edition of its Surface Mouse with integrated haptics, and you can read all about that here.
Microsoft is also bringing back the black color option for both of these smaller Surface devices, with platinum silver or violet colors available too. Both devices will also be sold to commercial customers, and the Surface Pro 12-inch will be available in an optional 5G configuration.

articles.title_zh: Meta's Muse rekindles fears over winners and losers as personal AI agent emerges
articles.content_orig:
The New York Times reporter Eli Tan using Meta Muse to buy movie tickets in San Francisco. Credit... Poppy Lynch for The New York Times
Reporting from San Francisco
Last week, I answered a call from an unknown number. “I reached Anthem Dental and am about to connect you,” a voice piped up.
The call was from an artificial intelligence “agent” created by Meta, which owns Facebook and Instagram. Ten minutes earlier, the A.I. agent had called my dental insurer, given it my member ID, answered a security question and waited on hold before transferring me to the representative — just as I had asked it to.
I was surprised by how much easier the agent had made it to deal with insurance. It was one of many tasks that I accomplished with Muse , the A.I. agent app that Meta unveiled this month.
Muse is the first consumer A.I. agent from a major tech company that has become publicly available. The tech industry sees agents as the next frontier, far more capable than chatbots. Agents can roam the internet, sign in to websites, fill out spreadsheets and make phone calls on behalf of people — and that’s just the start.
To test Muse, I experimented with it nonstop for two weeks, giving over many aspects of my life to it. I had to trust Muse with my most personal data, which included connecting it to my bank accounts and email. Then I had it perform dozens of day-to-day tasks, including ordering my groceries, scheduling my meetings and setting my fantasy football lineups.

articles.title_orig: Dolly Parton’s estate accuses her nephew of threatening violence and to destroy his aunt’s legacy
articles.title_zh: Dolly Parton’s estate accuses her nephew of threatening violence and to destroy his aunt’s legacy
articles.content_orig:
Judge grants restraining order against Dolly Parton's nephew Bryan Seaver
A judge in Nashville has granted a restraining order against Bryan Seaver.
Dolly Parton's nephew has been ordered to remain nearly a quarter of a mile away from any employee of her former manager.
The order was requested by Danny Nozell, manager of She's Alive LLC, a company created to oversee the late country icon's estate and legacy.
He recently filed a temporary restraining order in Nashville against Parton's nephew, Bryan Seaver, after firing him as head of security, alleging a campaign of extortion, intimidation and threats following Parton's death.
The order was granted by Davidson County Chancellor I'Ashea Myles.
Seaver needs to stay 1000 feet (304 metres) from any employee of She's Alive and cease communication with anyone connected to the company, The Tennessean reports.
Seaver, the son of Dolly's sister Cassie, announced Parton's death in a social media video. He was her head of security at the time she died.
Variety was first to publish a series of menacing text messages Seaver allegedly sent in connection with the ensuing dispute between him and She's Alive.
"I'm not an entertainment person. I'm a killer," reads one message in the filing. "I sold 27 million $ worth of ammunition and arms to the Haitian Police on day Dolly died. Entertainment is not my game. I have spent my career breaking things and spying on African and Arab leaders. And protecting Dolly."
Additional messages promised a podcast "dedicated to ruining Dolly's brand partnerships" if he wasn't paid.
"Her money better be bigger than I can make elsewhere or I'm going to f**k everyone."
In response, Seaver told TMZ nothing in the lawsuit was a threat and that he was only having "rage talk" on the phone with Nozell.
"I was talking frankly in a private way with Danny, who I thought was my friend, and he fancies himself a gangster," he stated.

articles.title_orig: Many voters see midterms as vote against Trump, new poll finds
articles.title_zh: Many voters see midterms as vote against Trump, new poll finds
articles.content_orig:
Many voters see midterms as vote against Trump, new poll finds
With less than six weeks until the November midterm elections, a plurality of American voters say their upcoming congressional vote will be "mainly a vote against President (Donald) Trump," according to a new Marist University poll.
In the NPR and PBS News-sponsored poll, released Sept. 23, 45% of registered voters described their midterm vote as primarily a "vote against President Trump than a vote for him."
A majority of independents, 54%, said their vote was "a vote against" the president, with an overwhelming majority of Democrats, 80%, sharing the same sentiment. Among Republicans, 35% said the president did not factor into their vote in November.
That plurality of voters coincides with a large Democratic lead in the generic congressional ballot. According to the newest poll, Democrats hold a lead of 12 percentage points over the GOP, up 2 points from the same poll in May.
According to Marist University, the poll was conducted among 1,280 respondents from Sept. 14 to Sept. 15 with a margin of error of 3.8 percentage points.
Democrats more trusted, poll shows
Voters’ rebuke of the president comes as his party looks to hold slim majorities in both the House and the Senate.
According to the poll, voters said they trusted Democrats over the GOP to manage the economy, foreign policy, gas prices, and, very narrowly, immigration. For immigration, 41% said they trusted Democrats while 38% gave Republicans the nod.
For Democrats, it is an 11-point improvement from 2024, when only 30% said they would do better than Republicans.
Voters’ trust in Democrats' handling of gas prices comes as the national average price of a gallon sits at $4.47, according to the AAA. That price marks an 11-cent jump from a week ago and a 38-cent increase from a month ago.
Trump approval staggers along
The September poll found Trump’s approval rating sitting at 39%, a 1-point improvement from its June poll. Despite the improvement, 53% of voters strongly disapproved of the president's job, which Marist University said shows an “electorate with hardened, high-intensity views rather than soft or persuadable ones.”
Trump’s approval rating in the new survey came on the heels of two bruising polls for the president.
On Sept. 22, a new Economist/YouGov poll found that his approval rating had fallen 5 points in a single week, from 40% to 35%, wiping out five straight weeks of gains in the same poll. That drop left the president just 2 points above the lowest rating he's ever recorded in the survey.
Then, a day before, on Sept. 21, an even worse poll saw Trump sink to the lowest approval rating of his political career in Reuters/Ipsos tracking. According to the poll, only 32% of Americans approved of Trump's job performance, a 3-point drop from the previous edition.
Trump’s 32% approval rating in the Sept. 21 poll set a new record low across both of his terms in office. Previously, Trump’s floor was 33%, which he reached in December 2017 and held for three consecutive weeks this August.
What do polling averages show?
While individual polls vary, major polling averages continue to place Trump in negative territory overall:
- RealClearPolitics (Sept. 23): 39% approve, 59.5% disapprove
- New York Times (Sept. 23): 37% approve, 60% disapprove
- Silver Bulletin (Sept. 23): 37.6% approve, 59.9% disapprove
Fernando Cervantes Jr. is a trending news reporter for USA TODAY. Reach him at fernando.cervantes@usatodayco.com and follow him on X @fern_cerv_.

articles.title_orig: Hacking group claims to have stolen thousands of FBI employee records
articles.title_zh: Hacking group claims to have stolen thousands of FBI employee records
articles.content_orig:
The FBI said Wednesday that it is investigating a notorious hacking group over its claims to have stolen data on agents.
“The FBI is aware of a cyber-criminal enterprise group claiming a compromise of the FBIJobs.gov portal and alleged impact to FBI employee personally identifiable information (PII),” the FBI said in a statement. “While the point of breach is still undetermined — whether a third-party or the FBI’s enterprise — we are actively and aggressively investigating this matter and working closely with those third-party providers that support FBIJobs.gov to mitigate any and all risk.”
The hacking group, ShinyHunters, a cyber-extortion outfit that routinely hacks companies to steal their data and threatens to publish it on the dark web if not paid, said Wednesday that it had hacked into the FBI’s jobs portal and used that access to steal a major tranche of sensitive files, including ones that detail individual agents’ personal information.
In a post on its website viewed by NBC News, ShinyHunters said the alleged hack was retaliation for a public service announcement about the group that the FBI posted in May.
“We were very disappointed to see an agency of your standing would resort to such circulation of disinformation in an attempt to ‘disrupt’ our operations, an effort that ultimately proved unsuccessful,” it said. It disagreed with the FBI’s characterizations in its PSA and said it would publish hacked data in a week if the PSA was not retracted.
A representative of the group claimed to NBC News that they hacked the FBI’s job portal Monday and then gained access to other agency programs, stealing between 2 and 3 terabytes of files. NBC News was not able to verify the extent of their claims. The job portal site is currently inaccessible.
An agency spokesperson said: “The FBI is aware of claims regarding unauthorized activity affecting FBIjobs.gov and is currently investigating.”
One former FBI agent confirmed to NBC News the authenticity of a sample document that includes sensitive personal information that ShinyHunters sent as evidence.
Cynthia Kaiser, the former deputy cyber director of the FBI and a senior vice president at the cybersecurity company Halcyon, told NBC News that the alleged breach was worrying, as exposing personal information on FBI agents, who often sign their names to court documents used to prosecute criminals, endangers them.
“This type of information could be used by criminals to target or physically harm FBI agents, personnel and their families,” Kaiser said. “So I get concerned when you start thinking about physical addresses, who people’s spouses are, all of that.”
Kaiser said that ShinyHunters was unlikely to be outright lying about its access but that like most cybercriminal extortionists, it tends to exaggerate its claims.
“You often see a mixture of truth and lies when you’re dealing with threat actors like this,” she said. “They’re trying to show people, ‘Look what I have. You’re so scared of what I might show next, so you should do exactly what I should tell you to do, right?’”
ShinyHunters is a loosely defined group, with members scattered around the globe. AI company Anthropic released one clue about its operations in a threat intelligence report earlier this month, when it said it had since December repeatedly disrupted clusters of ShinyHunters affiliates trying to use the company’s AI in their hacking operations.
While some cybercriminals can operate with relative impunity in countries that do not extradite to the U.S., the FBI does regularly arrest cybercriminals directly or with the help of law enforcement in countries friendly to the U.S.
Antagonizing the FBI might tempt the agency to make more of an effort to arrest ShinyHunters members, Kaiser said.
“That’s normally a recipe for a takedown. There’s going to be more resources against them,” she said.
The ShinyHunters spokesperson said it was aware of that risk.
“We have been working on this since the release of the FBI FLASH report they made on us in May. This was well planned and coordinated,” the spokesperson said.

Woody Harrelson Says Matthew McConaughey Family Mystery Is Finally Solved
Woody Harrelson has added a surprising new detail to the long-running mystery involving Matthew McConaughey's family. The actor says he now has what he considers proof about the connection between their parents. His claim comes as the longtime friends promote their new Apple TV+ series.
Woody Harrelson claims he has "definitive confirmation" his father had a sexual relationship with Matthew McConaughey's mother
Harrelson and McConaughey discussed the family mystery on the "New Heights" podcast. The actors appeared on Travis and Jason Kelce's show to promote Brothers, which premiered on Apple TV+ Wednesday. The series draws from the real story involving McConaughey's mother, Kay, and Harrelson's father, Charles Harrelson. Woody now says he has "definitive confirmation" about their past.
The story began during a trip to Greece involving McConaughey's family. Kay reportedly told Harrelson that she "knew" Charles, and the word came with a noticeable pause. Woody and Matthew have said the moment carried sexual meaning. That detail led to years of questions about whether the actors could actually share a biological father.
Harrelson said he believes his father and Kay were sexually involved. He told the Kelce brothers that he has "definitive confirmation," although he did not explain what convinced him. McConaughey has continued to avoid taking a DNA test. So, the actors have not publicly confirmed that they are biological brothers.
Harrelson also pointed to similarities between himself and McConaughey. He said he noticed certain habits or small mannerisms in Matthew even before they knew about the possible family connection. Those similarities added another layer to the unusual story. The two actors also share a close friendship and have worked together for years.
