articles.title_orig: China silent as US touts plan for AI safety alerts that omits tech experts
articles.title_zh: China silent as US touts plan for AI safety alerts that omits tech experts
articles.content_orig:
This week, the US and China, the two world leaders on AI, finally started talks meant to keep the whole world safe from emerging safety risks. But whether meetings between Donald Trump and Xi Jinping can lead to a reliable global governance framework for AI depends on how much the fierce rivals are actually willing to cooperate.
It’s clear Trump wants it to seem like discussions are going well. Before Trump and Xi meet on Thursday and Friday, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent announced that both sides had already discussed setting up a new AI safety notification mechanism. If China agrees to participate, that would create an open line for either side to send alerts when their country’s AI systems pose threats or behave unpredictably. The same channel, Bessent said, could allow the countries to share their “vision of common goals.”
However, the proposal comes at a time when China may not be ready to trust the US to have AI safety conversations that aren’t about limiting China’s capabilities. Not only has Trump steadily increased export controls that explicitly seek to block China from accessing technology to advance AI, but Congress is mulling bills that would cut the country off from more chips and hardware. Adding to tensions, just two weeks ago, Trump’s Justice Department accused six of China’s leading AI makers of stealing from US frontier labs, which China has strongly disputed.
Some US-China experts told Ars that there were concerns that China might cancel talks, but China seemingly isn’t taking offense to Trump’s rhetoric. Even Truth Social posts where Trump insists that America must dominate China on AI—declaring “WHOEVER WINS AI, WINS! We are leading China, and all others, and will continue to do so”—didn’t keep China from showing up.
Notably, China has yet to publicly acknowledge the proposed alert system. Even if China bought into the system, people familiar with Bessent’s plan told Politico that the plan to monitor safety alerts appears superficial, since it involves no officials with technical expertise who could be trusted to assess the urgency of risks described in communications.
Describing the significance of the arrangement, one source mocked the plan, saying “the scientific, technical term is BS.”
Sam Bresnick, a research fellow at a Georgetown University think tank called the Center for Security and Emerging Technology, monitors national security applications of AI and US-China tech competition. He agreed it’s a red flag that there’s no tech body of tech experts monitoring the channel.
“It’s an existing channel, which I think is better than creating a whole new channel,” Bresnick told Ars. But if both sides had tech experts, the US and China could have really high-level conversations about how they’re assessing risk. That’s particularly important when discussing military risks, Bresnick emphasized.
“I think it’s better than nothing for sure, but I don’t have a lot of confidence that that is going to make a major difference going forward,” Bresnick said.
Low expectations for Trump talks
Su Lian Jye, a chief analyst at a global technology research and advisory group called Omdia, told the South China Morning Post that the AI alerts may help “promote more transparency,” but it won’t make either side less wary of the other.
“I don’t think the dialog will remove all concerns and differences on distillation, pricing competition, and pacing,” Su said.
Praising the plan as a good start to open dialogues, Su suggested that much more cooperation would be needed to make the safety mechanism meaningful.
“Turning the proposal into an effective tool would require both countries to agree on risk classifications, notification triggers, response protocols, and regular review procedures,” he said.
Perhaps that will come up when Trump and Xi meet later this week, with AI supposedly at the top of the agenda.
It’s unclear what will be discussed, but critics concerned about the most urgent AI safety risks fear that Bessent’s announcement indicates that Trump has modest ambitions for the summit.
On CBS’s “Face the Nation,” US Representative Ro Khanna—the ranking Democrat on the US House Select Committee on Strategic Competition Between the United States and the Chinese Communist Party—suggested that talks between Trump and Xi should go much further than setting up a line between two officials with no tech expertise.
He argued Trump should be asking Xi for an international agreement that urgently includes “banning any recursive self-improving AI” and “safeguards so that AI can’t be misused by people for biological nuclear weapons.”
China suspicious of AI safety talks
Many experts described sharing safety alerts as a decent first step in improving US-China coordination on AI, which Trump’s incoming “AI czar” could then possibly build on.
Alvin Wang Graylin, a global technology strategist and digital fellow at Stanford Digital Economy Lab, has spent decades weighing geopolitical risks. Most recently, he’s advised governments and tech leaders on AI policy and global governance, including sharing recommendations on how to set up a notification system like the one Bessent proposed.
Graylin told Ars that he was surprised to see that such a “positive” development had already come out of this week’s talks with China. And it seemed encouraging that both countries already have another meeting scheduled in November.
“What that shows is that both sides are seeing value in the discussion,” Graylin said. “Otherwise, there would not be a follow-on.”
Graylin suggested the US and China share many AI risks. Not just the supposedly existential risk that AI leaders started recently claiming required a slowdown, but also risks from bad actors like hackers or terrorists wielding AI to attack either country’s infrastructure.
There’s much that the US and China can learn from each other if they talk seriously. Graylin said that China regularly audits AI models and could share knowledge from hundreds of audits, since the US has only just begun auditing AI. What China could gain from the US is perhaps more experience auditing frontier models.
“I think both sides are going to come to the realization” that controlling AI risk will “require cooperation,” Graylin said.
Bresnick suggested that ongoing talks could be an opportunity to “explore how each side views risks.” While the US has been combating public fears of uncontrollable AI, in China, “there’s just not the same fear right now about AI,” Bresnick said, largely because the state feels that it can control AI.
That may change as China’s advanced AI catches up to the US, Bresnick said. He expects that US-China discussions could ramp up in the next six months to a year, as China starts to see the same level of emerging capabilities.
However, for now, the very different way that China views risk may deter America’s biggest rival from coming to the table to talk about risks from terrorists or hackers, Bresnick said. Especially if the US continues tying the AI safety discussion to keeping America ahead.
When Trump or CEOs like Sam Altman advocate for American-led global AI standards, all China probably sees is the US wielding safety discussions as a way to lock in its advantage, he said. Those concerns may even render Bessent’s alert system useless in the long term if China feels that “AI safety” is a code word for suppressing Chinese AI.
“I think there are reasons [for China] to view this notification mechanism with suspicion,” Bresnick said.
Trump’s “deeply flawed” AI race
Graylin has warned that the US is too caught up in pushing a “deeply flawed” narrative about “winning” an “AI race” that most likely will benefit no one.
In reality, there are at least two races, one for intelligence and one for market dominance. Currently the US is making more money on frontier AI but is falling behind in the race for users globally. articles.title_orig: Clavicular's rise shows the manosphere is changing. His criminal charges raise new questions
articles.title_zh: Clavicular's rise shows the manosphere is changing. His criminal charges raise new questions
articles.content_orig:
Clavicular's rise shows the manosphere is changing. His criminal charges raise new questions
Clavicular, the controversial streamer who rose from the corners of the internet to the mainstream advocating for extreme tactics to achieve physical attractiveness, now finds his internet fame spilling into the courtroom.
Braden Peters, better known for his online moniker, has been charged in Massachusetts court with rape, drugging a person for sex and providing alcohol to an underage person, court records show.
Peters, 20, has become the visible face of the "looksmaxxing" movement. He’s gone to extremes such as hitting himself in the face with a hammer so his bones supposedly grow back sharper and taking small amounts of methamphetamine in an attempt to suppress his appetite. Offshoots of the trend, which are associated with the "manosphere," have ventured into sexist, misogynistic and racist philosophies, while Peters himself has drawn criticism for using racial slurs during his streams.
The viral nature of his controversial soundbites and short-form content helped usher what was once a niche subculture on obscure Reddit forums into the mainstream on TikTok, Instagram and Kik, where he’s collectively amassed more than 2.7 million followers. Now, the turn in his trajectory offers a window into the pitfalls of a movement drawing young men online in droves.
What is 'looksmaxxing,' the 'manosphere?'
"Looksmaxxing" is the process of maximizing one’s physical appearance through hygiene, fitness and style.
The term has gone mainstream and can have positive implications, such as getting healthy or working out more in the hopes of finding more confidence in the dating world.
However, the looksmaxxing movement has roots in online incel culture, which villainizes women, and has become a new subset of the "manosphere," a digital collection of websites, videos and social media that promote male supremacy and advocate for traditional gender roles.
How young men get sucked into 'looksmaxxing'
The combination of technology and the natural insecurities that arise during teenage years creates a "perfect storm" for innocuous sports and health spaces to tune young men into radical content, Gary Barker, the president of Equimundo: Center for Masculinities and Social Justice, an organization that advocates for healthy manhood, previously told USA TODAY.
"They’re going there with kind of innocent intentions, but without somebody else supporting them, that innocent intention can become a follower who drops their critical thinking," Barker said.
Looksmaxxing creators have become a modern extension for Gen Z and Gen Alpha. Among these creators, such as Kareem Shami, an early adopter who encourages "mewing," and Alex Costa, who focuses on "softmaxxing" with style and haircare, Clavicular has become the most extreme, advocating for surgical upgrades. In June, he livestreamed his rhinoplasty on Kick, undergoing four procedures ahead of Paris Fashion Week in what he called "Ascension Week."
As his looksmaxxing tactics have been more extreme, so have his far-right, sexist and racist rhetoric.
His streams often feature degrading language regarding women, and he was seen partying in Miami with Andrew and Tristan Tate, manosphere creator Sneako and far-right nationalist Nick Fuentes in January, where the group was filmed singing along to Ye’s "Heil Hitler."
On Sept. 4, Romanian prosecutors indicted 39-year-old Andrew Tate for allegedly trafficking minors, money laundering, sex with a minor and witness tampering, and his 38-year-old brother Tristan Tate for alleged complicity.
"The current version of the manosphere has become much more mainstream than it used to be," said University of Wisconsin-Madison public affairs professor Mariel Barnes, whose research focuses on backlash to gender equality and the manosphere. "You don't need to hide who you are anymore if you're a raging misogynist."
Extreme fringes of the manosphere have orchestrated or praised violent attacks against women, a trend Netflix’s 2025 crime drama "Adolescence" highlighted by following the story of a 13-year-old boy who was radicalized by misogynistic culture online.

articles.title_orig: Judge appears skeptical of Trump’s effort to ban news outlets from White House
articles.title_zh: Judge appears skeptical of Trump’s effort to ban news outlets from White House
articles.content_orig:
This story appeared in Today, Explained, a daily newsletter that helps you understand the most compelling news and stories of the day. Subscribe here.
Trump is bracing to lose his latest fight with the press
Trump’s lawyers said he barred three news outlets from the White House on security grounds. A judge seemed skeptical.
A hearing on President Donald Trump’s White House press ban ended without a ruling this afternoon — an admittedly anticlimactic outcome, but one that will likely change very soon.
The Trump-appointed judge in the case, Timothy Kelly, appeared skeptical of the administration’s arguments for banning CNN, MS NOW, and Politico from the White House grounds last week. Kelly said he would rule “as soon as possible.” Until then, the ban remains in place.
By all accounts, Trump’s case is a feeble one. While the Justice Department attempted to argue on Wednesday that the three outlets’ reporting jeopardized national security, Trump himself kind of gave the game away last week when he said he had singled these organizations out over what he characterized as negative and inaccurate stories.
The move sat poorly even with people and institutions you’d expect to be sympathetic to Trump: Fox News was one of several outlets that boycotted White House events this week to protest the ban, for instance.
And ahead of today’s hearing, Trump himself seemed primed to lose. In a Truth Social post on Monday, he promised he would “almost without question” appeal any decision against him.
This is all emblematic of how Trump has escalated his attacks on the news media in his second term: not just by insulting and demeaning the press, but also by weaponizing otherwise neutral-seeming rules.
Every administration has policies that regulate who can access the White House grounds and under what conditions, for instance. But in early 2025, the White House took control of the press pool — the rotating group of reporters that frequently travels with the president — and soon sought to exclude disfavored organizations.
More insidiously, Trump has mobilized regulatory agencies like the Federal Communications Commission against his perceived critics, in some cases even threatening to revoke the licenses of local TV stations that air coverage and commentary he disagrees with.
While no licenses have actually been suspended, the FCC has mysteriously pulled some up for unscheduled review. And just the prospect of government retaliation has been enough to force some content off the air: Just two weeks ago, the late-night comedy host Jimmy Kimmel said his show wouldn’t air a scheduled interview with Texas Senate candidate James Talarico because of the FCC’s new scrutiny of political content.
This playbook isn’t a Trump original, as my colleague Zack Beauchamp has explained. In fact, weaponizing broadcast regulations was also a favored technique of former Hungarian Prime Minister (and infamous strongman) Viktor Orbán, who successfully used licensing rules and other bureaucratic technicalities to force independent media outlets into submission.
Likewise, revoking the press credentials of critical reporters has long been a favorite tactic of Russian President Vladimir Putin, Nico Perrino, the executive vice president of the nonprofit civil liberties group Foundation for Individual Rights and Expression, said in a briefing on Wednesday: “These are things that are done by regimes that we do not want to emulate.”
Lest these comparisons get you down, however, recall that neither Hungary nor Russia has all the defenses that the US does. Defenses like, for example, an independent court system.
➨ Date a little differently. It’s not just your imagination: The search for love has become weirdly intolerant and antagonistic. One new survey finds that the percentage of singles with a must-have trait list they’re checking off has risen to a whopping 34 percent. Experts blame larger cultural changes, the rise of dating apps, and negative social media narratives. But you can fight back in your own dating life by letting your guard (and maybe your standards!) down a little bit.

articles.title_orig: Questions remain over China’s $17 billion U.S. ag purchase commitment
articles.title_zh: Questions remain over China’s $17 billion U.S. ag purchase commitment
articles.content_orig:
Questions remain over China’s $17 billion U.S. ag purchase commitment
Questions remain about China’s ag purchase commitments as the U.S. and China meet tomorrow.
“You never know in these high level discussions what you’ll walk out with.” says Justin Benavidez, the chief economist at the USDA.
Benavidez says China has been making progress on its 25 million metric ton soybean commitment, but what’s happening with the $17 billion in extra ag product purchases is unclear.
He says China’s relisting of U.S. beef plants for export is a positive development for trade barriers.
“Now, they’ve obviously put in place some tariff rate quota thresholds that are pretty aggressive and might, in turn, keep us out of the marketplace, to some extent, for beef exports. But I think the relisting of the plants was a positive, overall, story for beef.”
Seth Meyer with the University of Missouri’s Food and Ag Policy Research Institute says there’s still uncertainty about what products will make up those additional purchases.
“Is it other meats, is it ethanol, what counts under this, and how close will we get to that?” asks Meyer.
President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping are scheduled to meet on Thursday.
Benavidez and Meyer were part of the Ag Outlook Forum, sponsored by the Ag Business Council of Kansas City and Agri-Pulse, in Kansas City, Missouri this week.

articles.title_orig: Microsoft's New Surface Pro 12 And Surface Laptop 13 Feature Snapdragon X2 Plus Chips
articles.title_zh: Microsoft's New Surface Pro 12 And Surface Laptop 13 Feature Snapdragon X2 Plus Chips
articles.content_orig:
Microsoft's new Surface Pro 12 and Surface Laptop 13 feature Snapdragon X2 Plus chips
There's also a new haptic Surface Mouse on the way.
Microsoft's hardware business seems to be in disarray on all fronts, especially Xbox, but it's still trucking along with refreshed versions of its smaller Surface Pro 12 and Surface Laptop 13. The big change is the new Snapdragon X2 Plus chip, which aims to be a solid update from the slower Qualcomm chips powering those devices last year. As Microsoft's smallest PCs, the key for both the Surface Pro 12 and Laptop 13 is portability over raw power. These were also ostensibly low-cost devices last year, with launch prices below $1,000, but as with everything else, the RAMaggedon has bumped the Surface Pro 12-inch up to $1,150 and the Surface Laptop 13 to $1,199.
Design-wise, nothing has changed with either device. The Surface Pro 12-inch is still a small 12-inch tablet with a kickstand, and it can transform into a pseudo-laptop with the $150 Surface Pro keyboard (sold separately, as always, because Microsoft seems to hate smart consumer choices). The Surface Laptop 13, meanwhile, is the company's basic notebook design shrunk down to a 13-inch screen and 2.7-pound frame. Both systems also feature new 500-nit displays, which are 25 percent brighter than before.
I thought the 12-inch tablet was absolutely adorable when I reviewed it last year, and I'm hoping the new internals alleviate my performance concerns. Microsoft claims the Snapdragon X2 Plus chips deliver 60 percent better graphics than the last generation, as well as 95 percent faster on-device AI and 18 percent better battery efficiency. As for basic Office productivity work, the company says the new chip is 18 percent faster. The upgrades sound compelling for anyone who was interested in these smaller Surface devices, but couldn't stomach the major speed downgrade of the previous Snapdragon X chips. If you picked up one of these systems last year, though, it's probably worth waiting a bit longer to upgrade. And if you need more power, the larger 13-inch Surface Pro and Surface Laptop 13.8-inch are also available with newer Snapdragon X2 chips (and much higher pricing of their own).
The Surface Pro 12-inch is also launching together with Microsoft Ink Canvas, an "AI-powered, pen-first experience for sketching, annotating, generating images and summarizing text directly on the canvas," as the company describes. That doesn't sound particularly unique, but at least it's something to do with the Surface Slim Pen. The app will also be available on the Microsoft Store on October 13th for other Surface devices.
Alongside the PC hardware, Microsoft is launching a new $80 Surface Mouse, an ambidextrous mouse with haptic functionality. The company says you'll be able to feel certain Windows 11 interactions, like snapping a window or aligning objects. That's similar to what we've seen with the Logitech MX Master 4. It's an evolution of the previous Surface Mouse, which was notable for evoking Microsoft's classic Intellimouse design.
All of Microsoft's new Surface hardware will be available on October 13.

articles.title_orig: Treasury yields surge to near 20-year high as oil jumps back above $103 per barrel
articles.title_zh: Treasury yields surge to near 20-year high as oil jumps back above $103 per barrel
articles.content_orig:
The yields on U.S. Treasury bonds jumped Wednesday and oil prices rose, sending stocks tumbling as investors braced for the prospect of future Fed rate hikes.
The yield on the 10-year Treasury bond, which heavily influences consumer borrowing rates, especially mortgages, rose as high as 5.13%, its highest level since 2007. Indeed, the average 30-year fixed mortgage rate jumped to 7.26% on Wednesday, according to Mortgage News Daily. That’s the highest point since Jan. 13, 2025 — and of President Donald Trump’s second term.
The 10-year yield’s rise was its sharpest one-day jump since April 9, 2025, a week after Trump’s tariffs began roiling global markets, according to Dow Jones data.
Yields on 5- and 30-year Treasury bonds also hit levels that had not seen since before the 2008 global financial crisis.
Stocks fell in response to the rise in yields and oil prices. The Nasdaq Composite index ended the trading session down 1.13%, and the S&P 500 fell 0.75%. The Dow declined 352 points.
International Brent crude oil climbed 3.8% to end the day at $103.08 per barrel, while U.S. crude oil closed up 1.8% at $92.16. The rise in oil prices snapped a streak of five days of declines.
Rising oil prices often translate into higher bond yields due to the effect that higher energy costs can have on inflation more broadly.
One of the primary drivers of Wednesday’s rise in bond yields was the release of new economic data that revealed rising inflation.
Yields rise sharply when Treasury bonds sell off.
“US business activity growth accelerated for a fourth successive month in September to reach the fastest rate for over five years,” S&P Global reported in its latest purchasing managers index reading .
“Firms’ input costs have meanwhile jumped in September at the steepest rate for four years, with fuel and transport costs spiking higher thanks to the rise in oil prices seen during the month, which will add further to the upward pressure on selling prices and inflation in the coming months,” said Chris Williamson, chief business economist at S&P Global Market Intelligence.
Investors viewed the data as likely to increase the odds of multiple Federal Reserve interest rate hikes later this year and next. As of late Wednesday afternoon, market odds for a Fed rate hike in October were up to more 70%.
One Fed policymaker signaled that would likely vote in favor of another rate increase during the Fed’s Oct. 27-28 meeting.
“Risks to achieving our inflation target have increased, while risks to the labor market have receded,” Federal Reserve governor Michael Barr told a housing conference in Chicago.
“In my base case, further policy adjustments are likely to be needed to ensure inflation comes down to target in a timely fashion,” he said.
Crude oil trading desks Wednesday were focused on the latest developments in the Iran war.
A day earlier, the price of oil had fallen sharply after Trump said U.S. officials were holding talks with Iranian representatives at the U.N. General Assembly. But hopes that the talks would produce tangible results were dashed by a new report Wednesday that a cargo vessel had been “stuck by an unknown projectile” in the Strait of Hormuz.
Lying just off Iran’s southwestern coast, the critical chokepoint for global energy supplies has been under a military blockade for seven months.
Trump further shook energy markets Tuesday when he said he supported a ban on U.S. exports of diesel fuel.
“Let’s not send out the diesel,” Trump said to reporters at the U.N. “I’ve called for it within my people. I’ve been talking about it.”
Trump’s remarks sent European benchmark diesel futures higher by as much 7% early Wednesday.
But experts and energy industry groups warn that a ban on diesel exports would spell even higher gas prices for Americans.
“Removing U.S. diesel from the market could instead result in reduced refinery runs, global economic damage and even higher U.S. prices,” the American Petroleum Institute said in a statement.
Trump’s Energy Secretary Chris Wright also said a ban would not help to bring down prices.
“The blunt tool of banning diesel exports definitely doesn’t work,” he said Wednesday at an event in New York, according to Reuters .
Wright added at an event hosted by The New York Times later Wednesday that “nobody wants a full blanket ban or zero exports of diesel.”
“That’s not being discussed,” he said.
Inflation-sensitive stocks, such as travel companies and large technology firms, were the hardest hit by Wednesday’s reversal.
The S&P’s biggest sector loser was utilities, which contains many of the companies leading the AI data center boom. Higher interest rates could potentially add billions of dollars to the cost of building AI infrastructure.
The consumer discretionary and real estate sectors were also notable decliners.
Steve Kopack is a senior reporter at NBC News covering business and the economy.

articles.title_orig: Stocks fall as yields shoot higher, Nasdaq retreats from record: Live updates
articles.title_zh: Stocks fall as yields shoot higher, Nasdaq retreats from record: Live updates
articles.content_orig:
Traders work on the floor of the New York Stock Exchange (NYSE) in New York City, U.S., Sept. 16, 2026.
U.S. equities fell on Wednesday as Treasury yields marched higher amid concerns among investors that more interest rate hikes from the Federal Reserve may be coming down the pike.
Declines in utilities and consumer discretionary stocks led the broader market's fall, shedding more than 1% each.
Equities were weighed down by an increase in Treasury yields, which jumped after the latest purchasing managers' index readings came in hot. The yield on the 10-year Treasury note reached 5.135%, its highest level since July 2007. It also saw its biggest one-day move since April 7, 2025. The 2-year Treasury note yield hit its highest level since May 2024 at 4.947%.
2-year yield vs. 10-year yield, 1-day
"We have a lot of strength in corporate earnings, but we also have this inflationary pressure, and there's a tug of war there," Massimo Santicchia, head of U.S. equities at Procyon, said to CNBC, adding that it's "not just oil" that's driving inflation.
"It's broader, and it's particularly in the services sector," he said. "There's no way that the Fed is going to lower rates or pause at this point. Probably we're going to see maybe two, three rate increases."
Federal Reserve Governor Michael Barr said Wednesday that "further policy adjustments are likely to be needed" to get inflation under control.
"Economic growth is strong and the labor market is solid, but inflation is above our 2 percent target and not clearly trending toward target in a timely way," he said. "Moreover, risks to achieving our inflation target have increased, while risks to the labor market have receded."
Odds that the Fed would hike rates by a quarter percentage point in October stood above 66% following the developments, according to the CME FedWatch tool. That's up from 55.4% a day ago and just 8.8% one month ago.
During the annual United Nations General Assembly gathering in New York on Tuesday, President Donald Trump said that U.S. and Iranian officials met for three hours. He described it as a "very good meeting."
Earlier Tuesday in his address to the U.N., Trump said he has a "big decision" over whether to reach a deal with Tehran or "annihilate" the country.
In Tuesday's session, the Nasdaq hit a new all-time intraday high and closed at a record, while the Dow finished lower. The S&P 500 was roughly flat.
U.S. equities finished in the red on Wednesday.
The S&P 500 shed 0.75% to 7,706.03, while the Nasdaq Composite declined 1.13% to 26,936.04. The Dow Jones Industrial Average moved down 352.10 points, or 0.68%, to 51,511.59.
Oil industry warns a diesel export ban will increase fuel prices
A driver returns a fuel nozzle after refueling a vehicle with diesel fuel at a Chevron gas staying in Tracy, California, US, on Friday, Sept. 11, 2026.
David Paul Morris | Bloomberg | Getty Images
The oil industry has warned a diesel export ban will backfire and exacerbate the global fuel crisis as President Donald Trump weighs restrictions.
Trump appeared to back an export ban earlier this week, as he faces mounting political pressure to tackle rising fuel prices ahead of the midterm elections in November.
"I've said let's not send out the diesel. We make a lot of diesel," Trump told reporters Tuesday on the sidelines of the annual United Nations General Assembly. "I've called for it within my people. I've been talking about it."
All but two of the 11 S&P 500 sectors were falling in afternoon trading on Wednesday.
Energy led the way, rising about 1.1%. Industrials was the only other positive group on the day, up only marginally at about 0.2%.
Conversely, utilities was the biggest laggard, dropping 1.7%. Consumer discretionary and communication services weren't too far behind, notching a loss of 1.5% and 1.4%, respectively.
Market sees next Fed hike in October
Federal Reserve Board Governor Michael Barr speaks during a panel before the "Strengthening America's Economy Through Rural Investment: a Working Forum" hosted by the Federal Reserve Board of Governors, in Washington, D.C., U.S., April 14, 2026.
An October interest rate hike is very much on the table after a top Federal Reserve official Wednesday expressed support for one, and as fresh economic readings showed intensifying inflation pressures.
In remarks prepared for a housing conference in Chicago, Fed Governor Michael Barr said he thinks policymakers still have more work to do even after last week's quarter percentage point increase.
"In my base case, further policy adjustments are likely to be needed to ensure inflation comes down to target in a timely fashion," he said. "We want to support sustainable, durable growth in support of maximum employment, and price stability is crucial to that." Read more.
Stocks making big moves: McDonald's, Cracker Barrel Old Country Store, Worthington Enterprises
Check out some of the companies making the biggest moves midday:
McDonald's — CEO Chris Kempczinski said at an investor day event he expects high inflation and flat traffic will continue to weigh on the restaurant industry. The burger chain reported U.S. same-store sales growth of just 0.8% in its most recent quarter as traffic to its domestic restaurants fell. McDonald's shares fell more than 5% to their lowest since 2022.
Cracker Barrel Old Country Store — The restaurant chain climbed 5% after reporting fiscal fourth-quarter adjusted earnings per share of 99 cents, up from 74 cents last year. Revenue of $849.3 million beat the consensus Wall Street estimate of $834.6 million, according to FactSet data, while restaurant level profit margins, cost of goods sold and adjusted EBITDA margins were all better than expected.
Worthington Enterprises — The industrial manufacturing company rose 4% on an encouraging outlook from leadership. CEO Joseph Hayek said the company is seeing opportunities across its business, "including rapidly growing demand for our engineered [American Society of Mechanical Engineers] tanks used in liquid cooling systems for data centers." First-quarter adjusted earnings and revenue surpassed the Street's estimates, according to LSEG.
McDonald's slides to its lowest level since 2022 as growth plan fails to impress
McDonald's Corp. signage on the floor at the New York Stock Exchange (NYSE) in New York, US, on Monday, Aug. 25, 2025.
Michael Nagle | Bloomberg | Getty Images
McDonald's shares fell sharply Wednesday as the company unveiled a new multiyear growth plan alongside a warning from the company that high inflation and flat restaurant traffic are likely to persist.
CEO Chris Kempczinski told CNBC that the company is "not expecting things to change" as elevated costs and sluggish traffic continue to weigh on the industry.
Investors are not loving it: shares of McDonald's are down more than 5% in midday trading, on pace for their worst day since April 4, 2025 when they fell 5.7% and trading at their lowest levels since October 2022. The move extends a string of weakness: MCD is now on pace for its seventh straight weekly decline, which would mark its longest losing streak since August 2014.
Selig tells CNBC activity on "mentions" contracts are concerning
Michael Selig, President Donald Trump's nominee to serve as Commodity Futures Trading Commission chairman, testifies in a Senate Agriculture Committee hearing on his nomination on Capitol Hill, Nov. 19, 2025.
CFTC Chairman Michael Selig told CNBC's "Squawk on the Street" on Wednesday that activity on "mentions" contracts are "concerning."
The response comes after the CFTC informed some of its regulated entities on Tuesday that "mentions" contracts, where traders predict what one would say in a speech, televised event or earnings call, are susceptible to manipulation.
"I think a large number of these contracts have issues, and so we're going to take a hard approach in evaluating those," he said.

articles.title_orig: Iran's Pezeshkian accuses Trump of 'bullying mentality,' vows no surrender
articles.title_zh: Iran's Pezeshkian accuses Trump of 'bullying mentality,' vows no surrender
articles.content_orig:
Seven months after the United States and Israel launched a war on Iran, the Iranian president stood on a podium in New York to tell President Donald Trump that the Islamic Republic “will not bow down.”
As his country confronts its gravest existential war, and amid Trump’s threats of “annihilation” and mounting economic strain at home, Iran’s Masoud Pezeshkian told world leaders attending the United Nations General Assembly that Iran will not yield on its nuclear program, missile defenses or control of the Strait of Hormuz, the vital waterway through which a fifth of the world’s oil once flowed.
“We cannot let some have free access and gain their interest from a waterway while at the same time using that waterway to impose their aggressions upon us, to impose insecurity upon us, to forbid us access to our own waterways,” Pezeshkian said.
The Iranian president used the world stage to deliver Tehran’s demands and Iran’s core message to Trump, who has sought through war to defeat the Islamic Republic. Trump has boasted that the United States has “blown up” nuclear sites in Iran, and he has claimed control over the Strait of Hormuz. From the same podium on Tuesday, he said he was considering whether to “annihilate the Islamic Republic” and drive it “into hell.”
Pezeshkian’s address was among the most anticipated speeches at this year’s United Nations gathering, and delivering it on American soil was a rare historic moment: a foreign leader holding forth in an enemy country still at war with his own.
Despite Washington’s early forecasts that the fighting would be brief, the US-Israeli war on Iran has instead dragged on, turning a military operation that began with the killing of the Islamic Republic’s supreme leader, Ayatollah Ali Khamenei, into months of regional instability and one of the defining foreign policy legacies of Trump’s presidency.
One of Pezeshkian’s key messages offered a glimpse into how the Islamic Republic seeks to set its postwar regional stance, telling Iran’s neighbors that its future security must be guaranteed or the entire region will have to “live under insecurity together.”
The message carried an implicit threat, according to one expert.
“Iran was presenting regional security as indivisible, signaling that continued pressure and conflict would impose costs across the region,” Sanam Vakil, director of the Middle East and North Africa program at London’s Chatham House think tank, told CNN.
But the message also signals that Iran knows it will need to find a way to coexist with the rest of the region, according to another expert, Hamidreza Azizi, a senior analyst at the International Crisis Group.
“This reflects an understanding that, at the end of the day, Iran will need to find an arrangement for peaceful coexistence with its neighbors,” Azizi said.
Pezeshkian delivered his speech at the UN a day after Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi held at least two hours of talks in New York with Trump’s peace envoy Steve Witkoff, the first sign of diplomacy between the two nations since an ill-fated agreement was signed more than three months ago.
Following Pezeshkian’s remarks, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said those talks did not yield any major breakthrough, indicating the Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) from earlier this year was no longer on the cards.
A plan in June for further negotiations between Iran and the United States never came to fruition. The conflict flared instead, leaving the region sinking deeper into uncertainty over how the war would end. At home, Pezeshkian and the Iranian officials who engaged Washington diplomatically have faced scrutiny from rival hard-line factions, which regard any agreement with Trump as tantamount to surrender.
“The foreign minister must explain on which authorization was his meeting with the representative of the aggressor enemy conducted?” Ebrahim Rezaei, a hard-line lawmaker, asked Wednesday after Araghchi met Witkoff.
Pezeshkian has also drawn criticism from hard-liners for attending the meeting in New York.
“His critics expressed concern that if … he signaled any intention to compromise to the outside world, this would be interpreted as a sign of weakness and desperation and would therefore be counterproductive for Iran, which wants to end the war on its own terms,” Azizi of the Crisis Group said.
As Pezeshkian and Araghchi delivered Iran’s demands to the world and a message of coexistence to the region, security officials back home announced a more hard-line position in Iran’s negotiating tactics.
Iran’s Supreme National Security Council chief, Mohsen Rezaei, told state media in an interview broadcast around the same time as Pezeshkian’s speech that the Islamic Republic will adopt a new framework when negotiating with the US that will require Washington to take the first step.
“Under this new framework, the era of rhetoric and negotiations for their own sake has come to an end,” Rezaei said in the interview. “Any future talks, or the reopening of the Strait of Hormuz, will be contingent upon Washington’s full implementation of Iran’s requirements as a precondition.”
His remarks perhaps not only sent a message to Washington but were also aimed at assuaging hard-liners skeptical of the Iranian officials negotiating in New York.
Yet as Iran conducted diplomacy at the UN and signaled future coexistence with the region, Oman’s Maritime Security Center said a ship was targeted near the Strait of Hormuz, killing one person.
“Vessels are advised to transit with caution,” the UK Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) center said.

articles.title_orig: Seahawks' Macdonald apologizes to Broncos' Payton for comments
articles.title_zh: Seahawks' Macdonald apologizes to Broncos' Payton for comments
articles.content_orig:
Seattle Seahawks head coach Mike Macdonald told reporters Wednesday that the viral story he shared about Denver Broncos head coach Sean Payton accusing the Seahawks of cheating during the 2024 season wasn't intended for public use.
The 39-year-old Macdonald, now in his third season at the helm in Seattle, said he apologized to Payton for the Graham Bensinger interview clip.
Macdonald also acknowledged that he's "got to be better in that moment" and remember that he's always responsible for his words, regardless of the situation.
#Seahawks HC Mike Macdonald says he called Broncos HC Sean Payton to apologize after his Spygate story went public (when it was meant to remain private):
“It’s a lesson learned. … I’m responsible for what I say.” https://t.co/8oT85eFIFE pic.twitter.com/Ud2B10xojP
In the clip, which circulated widely across social media on Tuesday, Macdonald divulged how, long after the Seahawks defeated the Broncos 26-20 in Macdonald's first-ever regular-season game as a head coach back in 2024, Payton "basically threatened to come out publicly and do a whole Patriot Spygate type of thing."
Payton eventually heard that Macdonald and his staff had gathered an assortment of Broncos plays Denver fans had recorded during training camp practice and posted to social media, Macdonald explained to Bensinger. Macdonald said that, since those videos were public, Seattle used them to its advantage, scouting every one of them before the season opener. That methodology isn't unheard of in today's NFL.
Miami Dolphins head coach Jeff Hafley revealed earlier this month that, when he hired former Philadelphia Eagles offensive coordinator Kevin Patullo, he discovered that Patullo had "half" of Hafley's pressures on tape from fans videoing Green Bay Packers training camp in the lead-up to the 2024 campaign, Hafley's first as Packers defensive coordinator. Hafley noted he deployed a pressure in that season's opener that he had never run, "and they knew it was coming," and "[Patullo] said he saw that pressure on video." The Eagles won that Week 1 game 34-29 in Brazil.
As for Payton's suspicions, Macdonald said the renowned offensive coach called Seahawks general manager John Schneider and, according to Macdonald, expressed that he "thought it was a Michigan thing where we had a plant and the whole thing."
Macdonald continued: "So we had to counter with him to say like, 'Hey, look, if you come out of this, we're going to sue you because it's not true.'"
Payton ultimately let it go, Macdonald said.
He then added: "It was like the Cold War. [Payton] was like, 'I'm going to hit the button. I'm going to hit the button.' [We were like,] 'No, we're going to hit the button.' So none of us hit the button."
That candid exchange between Macdonald and Bensinger took place on set where the rest of the interview apparently occurred; however, it seemed as though Macdonald was especially relaxed and informal in the way he was telling the tale. The clip's camera angle was notably unorthodox as well, with the mic and lighting fixtures in view.
When asked Wednesday if he thought he was simply shooting the breeze with Bensinger before the cameras were rolling, Macdonald said, "Yeah."
"It's something that I didn't intend for public use," Macdonald said earlier in his news conference, "but it just felt like it was the most appropriate thing to reach out to Sean and really just apologize to him for having that end up be public where it wasn't meant to.
"It's something that [the Broncos] have to deal with in real time that wasn't really on their end. So that's really where you're like, 'Crap.' But it's a lesson learned."
He went on: "Honestly, I got to be better in that moment for understanding like, look, I'm responsible for what I say really no matter the circumstance, whether you're mic'd up, whether you're not, whether you have a certain type of understanding. So I fell short in that moment. So it stings for me, frankly, but it's something that I'm definitely going to learn from. And just a good example that we just got to take responsibility for the things that we say."
Macdonald conveyed that Payton was gracious in his response to the apology.
"Sean was great," Macdonald said. "I respect the heck out of him and his program, always have. He's a phenomenal football coach. It's been great to get to know him at the owners meetings the last couple years, and he was awesome.
"So I know we're both looking forward to moving forward from it, but I really appreciate how he handled it."
Payton: 'He and I are good'
Payton, a Super Bowl-winning coach like Macdonald, confirmed the two spoke Tuesday night.
"He and I are good," Payton said at his Wednesday news conference. "Lord knows, I've been in his position where you're talking about something ... and the story is three years ago. Now, I don't know Mike at that time really, but I know [John Schneider] really well. And, so, I'm sure my initial call to John wasn't pleasant, but I would say this, in talking with him, it allowed us to figure out how to handle our training camp relative to just videos.
"And I don't think anything was intentional by fans. You know what I mean? But at first, you're kind of thinking, man, how could … ? And then we did some research online of what was available, and that's kind of how we changed our policy."
So, in that way, the whole kerfuffle actually helped the Broncos "to some degree," Payton said.
A reporter inquired if Payton originally thought the Seahawks taped Denver's plays, not fans. He conceded he didn't know back then.
"So obviously I called shooting before I started looking. And I could only do that with John because, again, he's someone I'll have a beer with at the [NFL] combine. I consider him a good friend. But it was eye-opening relative to just, 'Alright, we got to be better in this area.'"
Payton went as far to say that Denver is pulling for Macdonald's Seahawks, "except for one game" (the teams will face off on "Thursday Night Football" in Week 6). After all, Seattle's playing the AFC West this season, so it could hand the Broncos' three divisional foes losses.
"Like I said, the conversation last night was good," Payton said, alluding to his talk with Macdonald. "I have a ton of respect for him, and that's it."

articles.title_orig: Donald Trump to greet Xi Jinping in rare airport welcome at start of three-day US visit - live updates
articles.title_zh: Donald Trump to greet Xi Jinping in rare airport welcome at start of three-day US visit - live updates
articles.content_orig:
US President Donald Trump will soon greet Xi Jinping in a rare airport welcome as the Chinese leader's plane touches down ahead of a three-day visit to the US
Edited by Oliver O'Connell and Johanna Chisholm with Bernd Debusmann Jr reporting from Andrews Air Force Base
Plane carrying Chinese leader touches downpublished at 22:46 BST
The Air China plane carrying Chinese leader Xi Jinping, his wife Peng Liyuan and other delegates has touched down at 17:39 local time at Joint Base Andrews, where US President Donald Trump will greet them.
What we know about the plane carrying China's leaderpublished at 22:40 BST
Image source, Getty Images
When the US president travels, they have Air Force One, one of the most recognisable aircraft in the world.
As it comes into view above Joint Base Andrews, Xi Jinping's plane is similar in many ways - it's almost always a Boeing 747 made up will all the bells and whistles required for the Chinese leader's travel. But it's less known to the world, and that's because it's not always the same plane.
Unlike the US, the Chinese government doesn't have an aircraft (or multiple) just for official presidential travel. Rather, Xi uses a 747 from an the Air China fleet of planes.
Chinese officials have told media that this measure is to reduce waste by making use of existing aircraft. The country's Air Force inspects the plane and modifies it to suit the president's needs, according to Chinese media, including removing seats to make space for sofas and beds.
Otherwise, little has been made public about the aircraft, though it's usually seen with an official flag near the door where the Chinese leader exits.
Are American attitudes towards China warming?published at 22:32 BST
Bernd Debusmann Jr White House reporter
China is often painted as an adversary and potential enemy by prominent Americans, both in and out of government. But Trump’s lavish welcome comes at a time when American attitudes towards China appear to be warming.
A recent poll by the Chicago Council on Global Affairs found that 41% of Americans see China’s territorial ambitions as a threat to the US. But that number is down from 52% in 2022.
More than half of Americans - 57% - believe the US should cooperate and engage with Beijing. Notably, that statistic cuts across the US political spectrum. Of Republicans who do not identify as Maga, 57% favour cooperation, as do most Democrats, both moderate and liberal.
However most Maga Republicans - 63% - favour limiting US relations with China - putting the president’s most loyal base at odds with Trump’s efforts to cosy up to Xi.
Trump and Melania await Xi Jinping's arrivalpublished at 22:24 BST
President Trump and First Lady Melania Trump are escorted from the presidential Marine One helicopter to a separate vehicle where they await Xi's arrival
Trump and Melania can be seen waiting inside The Beast, a heavily armoured presidential state care
A long motorcade awaits the arrive of Chinese leader Xi Jinping
Airfield buzzing with activity ahead of arrivalpublished at 22:20 BST
Bernd Debusmann Jr White House reporter
The arrival is still a little while away, but Joint Base Andrews has begun buzzing with activity.
A series of black SUVs and limos are parked near the tarmac, and the Air Force band has begun marching in formation onto the tarmac. It's hard to hear over the wind and a circling helicopter, but we can hear their drums and the faint commands of the officer giving directions. Other formations from the other services - including the Space Force subsequently joined as well, with rifles on their shoulders.
By the cannons, a group of blue Airmen in formal dress uniforms appears to be receiving instructions, and the honour guard that will meet Xi's aircraft is standing to my right. One of its members, from the US Army, is holding a US flag. Two members down the line, a member of the Marine Corps is holding a Chinese flag.
'Every detail, I was involved' - Melania Trump says about state visitpublished at 22:12 BST
US First Lady Melania Trump says she has been involved intimately with the planning of the itinerary for the visitors from Beijing.
"Every detail, I was involved," she told Fox News in an interview. She says Trump made the decision to personally greet Xi himself at the airport "because they have a great relationship" but she has involved in the other major components of the visit such as the state dinner.
"There is a lot of detail that comes into the plan, there is protocol that you need to follow" she said.
Aside from the arrival ceremonies at the White House, Mrs Trump has also planned a visit to the Smithsonian National Museum of Asian Art with her Chinese counterpart Peng Liyuan to show the cultural connections between the US and China.
The landmark visit will end on a historical note at the National Archives building where the couples will view important national records including those of "significant to the American and Chinese relationship," the White House says.
President Xi Jinping, with his wife First Lady Peng Liyuan
During their last visit in Beijing, Donald Trump was
accompanied by a posse of tech executives from some of America's largest firms –
including Apple's Tim Cook, Tesla's Elon Musk and Nvidia's Jensen
The South China Morning Post reports that Xi Jinping plans
to mirror the delegation Washington sent last May.
But the exact names of which executives the Chinese
leader plans to arrive with on Wednesday afternoon have yet to be confirmed.
His wife, Peng Liyuan, is confirmed to be travelling with Xi
and the two will return to China on Friday.
Born in Beijing in 1953, he is the sixth child of Xi
Zhongxun, a Communist revolutionary who helped establish the People's Republic
of China. His father eventually became a senior party leader and vice premier.
As a young child, Xi attended prestigious schools and
enjoyed privileges unavailable to most families.
Then politics turned against his family. In the early 1960s,
Xi's father was accused of being part of an "anti-party" clique,
banished to the countryside to work in a factory and purged from the party.
As the son of someone deemed to be a
"counter-revolutionary", teenage Xi was forcibly sent to a
re-education facility. Heeding the calls of then leader Mao Zedong to go to the
villages and learn from the peasantry, 15-year-old Xi headed to the countryside
with millions of other city students.
At 22, he left the countryside to study chemical engineering
at Tsinghua University, one of China's best academic institutions. After
graduating, he worked as a local official. His father's rehabilitation after
Mao's death helped Xi land positions in the central government and the
military, building relationships within the party.
In 2007, after a brief stint as top leader in Shanghai, Xi
joined the Politburo Standing Committee, China's top decision-making body.
years later, he succeeded Hu Jintao as the leader of the Communist Party.
US military on full display for Xipublished at 21:39 BST
Bernd Debusmann Jr White House reporter
Just a few moments ago, I stepped out onto the tarmac at Joint Base Andrews. It's unlike anything I've seen here over dozens of flights in and out with the White House.
Two sets of large risers have been set up for cameras, one each for US and Chinese media. About a dozen American TV crews are there. Some are from the major networks, and a large representation from conservative, Maga-adjacent media outlets.
To the left of the risers on the tarmac, I counted a dozen or so combat aircraft, both older F-16s and newer F-22s, among the most advanced fighter jets in the US arsenal.
To the right of the risers, four ceremonial cannons have been set up for the arrival. Uniformed military personnel are currently milling around.
Normally, there is very little fanfare to arrivals and departures here. Trump gets here, he either talks or he doesn't, and onto the aircraft he goes.

articles.title_orig: Where Is the U.S. Beating China on A.I., and Where Is It Lagging?
articles.title_zh: Where Is the U.S. Beating China on A.I., and Where Is It Lagging?
articles.content_orig:
About two years ago, education entrepreneur Boris But had what he calls a “penny-drop moment” – that, like countless others in China, his company needed to embrace AI before it was made obsolete by it.
His clients, well-off parents looking to send their children to study overseas, had begun arriving in his office reeling off information and opinions gleaned not from rival firms, but from chatbots.
In response, he started developing his own AI study tool, concluding: “If you can’t beat them, join them.”
The pace and quality of AI development in China is second only to the United States, with the two superpowers locked in an intensifying rivalry as the stakes rise with each new model’s capabilities.
Analysts generally agree that frontier, or cutting-edge, US models are still some way ahead of their Chinese counterparts.
But over the last few weeks the mood music from Silicon Valley has been decidedly sombre, as insider after insider has warned of the potential catastrophes that could result from “loss of control” of the most advanced AIs.
And last Saturday Anthropic chief executive Dario Amodei pitched a “worldwide pacing of the frontier” – something he said would “require cooperation with China”.
“China is definitely not receptive” to a slowdown on US firms’ terms, though, said Lian Jye Su from technology research group Omdia.
For the government, AI is a “core sovereignty capability”, and Beijing will not want to jeopardise the progress made in closing the gap with US frontier models.
“It sees these calls [for a slowdown] as a bid to lock in US advantage,” said Su.
Amodei made this explicit, mentioning China specifically when arguing it was key “to keep democracies’ AI lead over autocracies as large as possible”.
He advocated for measures including continued export controls to China on advanced chips and machinery – the existence of which some argue already amounts to a forced unilateral “pacing”.
China’s foreign ministry responded to Amodei’s piece by saying “fearmongering, confrontation and vicious competition will only disrupt the process of global AI governance”.
However, several analysts told the Guardian it would be a mistake to assume this suggested a rejection of the broader concerns raised by the essay.
This week China released the third iteration of its AI safety governance framework – a document that functions as a “mapping of the AI risk landscape and roughly what one should do about it”, said Gabriel Wagner, a researcher at Concordia, a Beijing-based AI safety consultancy.
Included in the updates are the risks posed by agents, the cybersecurity threats from frontier models and the issue of recursive self-improvement – an as-yet hypothetical scenario where AI becomes advanced enough to improve itself.
“In many ways, I think there is more common ground than people might assume between what Amodei is saying and what the Chinese government is saying,” said Wagner.
That contrasts with US president Donald Trump, who this week called fears AI could wipe out humanity a “hoax”.
Trump is set to meet counterpart Xi Jinping in Washington next week, with AI expected to make the agenda, though analysts are sceptical a major breakthrough will happen.
The ruling Communist party, finely attuned to risks to its political control, has been proactive in ensuring the new technology has developed within boundaries set by the state.
Centralised authority over critical infrastructure and commercial activity means China is generally better placed than the United States “to address any AI disaster”, said Omdia’s Su.
However, Chinese companies do less voluntary monitoring and evaluation work than US ones, said Leia Wang from the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace (CEIP).
Neither government seems prepared for a loss-of-control incident like those outlined over the last few weeks, she said.
China’s regulation, though, is “iterative … they are quick to adapt and release new measures”, she added.
China has had an algorithm registry since 2022, but warnings on agents released this year suggest a switch in focus “from controlling what AI says to controlling what it does”, per Concordia AI.
Beijing also issued national regulations this year aimed at curbing emotional dependency on companion AIs.
At the same time, AI is being actively encouraged across the economy to promote growth, enshrining this goal in its latest Five Year Plan.
Local governments are offering funding and low rents to companies to help achieve this – entrepreneur But was recently invited to pitch his company, Hampshire Education, to a small city three hours from Shanghai set on establishing a reputation as a tech hub.
Factories across the country’s huge manufacturing base are being encouraged to convert their processes into the AI era.
“Safety and controllability are certainly major concerns, and they are actively discussed,” said a representative for Black Lake Technologies, an industrial agent platform that says it has worked with 40,000 factories globally.
“But in manufacturing, these concerns tend to be much more concrete and operational … what companies care most about is whether the AI is reliable.”
Daily life in China is already highly digitised, with traditionally less discourse around data privacy helping with widespread adoption.
For example, digital health service A-fu, which features AI chatbot versions of prominent doctors trained on real clinical studies, recently hit 150 million users.
“Most people treat AI as an already-useful everyday tool, not an abstract threat, so the practical attitude is to live with it,” said Ni Tao, founding editor of tech website yangtzeer.com.
“There is real anxiety about jobs and misinformation, but it coexists with a strong belief that China must master AI rather than slow down.”

articles.title_orig: Fox News, NYT, AP and other media outlets jointly condemn Trump’s media ban
articles.title_zh: Fox News, NYT, AP and other media outlets jointly condemn Trump’s media ban
articles.content_orig:
Judge skeptical of Trump's White House ban on CNN, MS NOW and Politico
Washington — A federal judge on Wednesday signaled he is skeptical of President Trump's ban on CNN, MS NOW and Politico from White House grounds, saying in a hearing that the outlets were not given due process before their access was cut off.
Judge Timothy Kelly of the U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia heard arguments from the attorneys for the news outlets and the Justice Department in the dispute. Mr. Trump announced last week that the outlets were banned from the White House for their reporting. All three filed suit on Monday and sought a temporary restraining order, asking Kelly to immediately restore their employees' access to the White House complex.
Kelly pointed to two cases in the U.S. Court of Appeals for the D.C. Circuit that serve as precedent: a case known as Karem v. Trump from 2022, and another known as Sherrill v. Knight that was decided in 1977. Those cases established the precedent that the Fifth Amendment's right to due process applies when the White House tries to revoke a journalist's access.
"I think it is fair to say" that the process laid out in those two cases "wasn't followed here," Kelly said in Wednesday's hearing.
In a filing late Tuesday ahead of the hearing, the Justice Department said government lawyers submitted letters to the three outlets telling them their access was revoked. The letters claimed that the news outlets have "exhibited behavior in violation of the standards of professionalism and decorum expected of those given access to the White House Complex, including by trafficking in verifiable falsehoods about national security and other issues, and publishing sensitive or classified information."
The White House press office gave each of the news organizations until Friday at 5 p.m. to respond to the decision to revoke their credentials.
But Kelly pressed the Justice Department about the timing of the letters, noting that the news outlets only received notice about appropriate conduct after losing their credentials.
"I don't know how a letter that they got after the pass was revoked could provide them with the kind of standards that they would have to conform their conduct to. It's a piece of paper they got saying, 'You've already violated this,'" the judge said.
Ted Boutrous, an attorney representing the news outlets, told the judge that the letters "completely do not reflect what the president himself has said" and did not "even [come] close to conforming with due process or the First Amendment."
"The letters announced after-the-fact standards," Boutrous said.
Boutrous also took issue with the government's notion that there are national security issues at play, saying that assertion was a "post hoc" justification and "not legitimate." He said the government views national security as a "talisman" and "magic words."
"They're literally arguing that reporters shouldn't scrutinize national security decisions and activities by the government," he said, referring to the Justice Department's argument. "That's what the First Amendment baked into the Constitution — that journalists and the press could hold government officials accountable, serve as a check on them."
Boutrous noted that Mr. Trump only mentioned national security as a justification for revoking the journalists' access on Monday after the news organizations filed their lawsuit, saying it was like a "lightbulb went off" to raise it as an issue.
But Michael Velchik, a lawyer at the Justice Department, argued that "access to the White House is a privilege, not a right," and rejected Boutrous' argument that the president was discriminating against the news outlets based on the content of their coverage.
He noted that Mr. Trump frequently criticizes members of the media, including from outlets like ABC News and the New York Times, which continue to have access to the White House.
Reporters "can't have a get-out-of-jail-free card" if they can find a social media post criticizing them, Velchik said.
Velchik also argued that the president should be allowed to "take immediate action" to protect national security by swiftly banning the reporters.
Kelly closed the hearing without issuing a ruling from the bench, but said he would make a decision "as soon as I can."
Mr. Trump's ban had an immediate impact not only on each outlet's ability to access the White House grounds, but also CNN's participation in the White House television pool, which also includes four other outlets: CBS News, ABC News, NBC News and Fox News.
CNN was supposed to travel with Mr. Trump to New York on Monday for the United Nations General Assembly as part of the press pool, but was removed from the trip because of the ban. As a result, the four other networks suspended the television pool altogether in support of CNN.
The five-network television pool captures footage of the president that is then distributed to the other members of the TV pool and their affiliates and subscribers. Only these networks have set up and maintained the physical infrastructure to transmit footage from the White House and when traveling with the president to affiliates.
Chinese President Xi Jinping is set to arrive in Washington, D.C., later Wednesday, but the major television networks in the pool are not providing coverage of Mr. Trump's activities because of the ban.

articles.title_orig: US open to extending China trade truce, or bigger deal, Bessent says after meeting with He
articles.title_zh: US open to extending China trade truce, or bigger deal, Bessent says after meeting with He
articles.content_orig:
The U.S. is open to discussing shared risks with China in upcoming AI talks this weekend, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent told Axios.
Why it matters: The Trump administration has flatly rejected calls from industry to pace or slow down the development of AI, citing a fierce race against China.
Bessent's scheduled meeting with Chinese Vice Premier He Lifeng could provide an opening for talks on U.S.-China AI safety cooperation.
"The United States remains the leader in AI. And we are open to discussions on avoiding shared risks and avoiding bifurcation of our two systems. We expect our discussions to cover both open and closed weight models," Bessent said in a statement to Axios.
"Bessent and [United States Trade Representative Jamieson Greer] are the point guys on China. So it makes sense the secretary is in this position," a senior administration official said.
Driving the news: There will be multi-hour meetings in New York City, focused on AI, trade, rare earths, and other economic issues, building on previous discussions held in cities around the world, sources familiar said.
The agenda will remain flexible to allow for substantive discussion across the range of relevant issues, sources added.
Possible working-level meetings will continue into Monday, sources said.
Catch up quick: Bessent has played a key role in the Trump administration's AI agenda.
He was among the few cabinet members who flanked President Trump during a G7 press conference in June, where top AI CEOs and the administration discussed a U.S.-led effort to coordinate global AI standards.
Bessent also helped cool Anthropic's relations with the administration following a fallout with the Pentagon and is viewed as a reasonable actor who is trusted by the private sector and critical infrastructure operators, sources familiar have previously told Axios.
Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick led high-profile AI discussions during the G20 summit in North Carolina earlier this month, while Bessent is taking the lead on talks with China.
The big picture: Bessent's meetings in New York come days before Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping's summit in Washington on Sept. 24.
AI CEOs have been calling for U.S.-China coordination on safety standards.
"All parties should jointly promote the open and inclusive development of AI for good and for all," the Chinese Foreign Ministry said this week, while pushing back on U.S. AI companies' calls to slow down and warning against "fear-mongering."
The bottom line: While a major breakthrough in U.S.-China safety cooperation remains a tall order, Bessent's involvement signals room for engagement on AI between the competing countries.

articles.title_orig: Trump ready to ban diesel gas exports to lower costs at home – something his own energy secretary says could backfire
articles.title_zh: Trump ready to ban diesel gas exports to lower costs at home – something his own energy secretary says could backfire
articles.content_orig:
Trump ready to ban diesel gas exports to lower costs at home – something his own energy secretary says could backfire
If implemented, it would be the first restriction on American energy exports in over a decade
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article
Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.
President Donald Trump is preparing to institute a 90-day ban on diesel exports in a bid to bring down soaring prices — despite opposition from Energy Secretary Chris Wright and industry insiders, according to a new report.
The prohibition, which would be the first restriction on American energy exports in over a decade, could be announced in the coming days, Politico reported. The hope among administration officials is that, by redirecting diesel bound for Asia or Europe back into the U.S., it could provide relief at the pump ahead of the midterm elections. The White House described the story as “fake news.”
Global energy prices have risen dramatically amid the ongoing Iran war, largely due to the closure of the Strait of Hormuz, a critical trade route. On Wednesday, the average national price for a gallon of diesel stood at $6.52, up from $3.69 one year ago, according to AAA.
A number of top officials, including Wright and Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, as well as oil industry executives, have balked at the possibility of a 90-day ban.
“The blunt tool of banning diesel exports definitely doesn’t work because the U.S. exports a lot of diesel,” Wright said during a discussion this week, according to Politico.
“We’re the largest diesel exporter in the world, but that same refinery that produces diesel also produces gasoline and jet fuel,” he continued. “So, if you can’t export the diesel that comes out of our refineries when you run out of places to store it, and you have to reduce U.S. refining, which would put upward pressure on gasoline prices and jet fuel prices.”
After being informed of the plan by Wright on Tuesday, energy CEOs quickly telephoned the White House to push back against the ban, an administration energy adviser told the outlet, adding: “It’s a terrible idea.”
One reported concern is that the 90-day ban could be extended. Another is that it could create a precedent for further government intervention in the private sector down the line.
An industry official told Politico that the fate of the proposal may come down to whoever is “the last person in the room” with the president.
Despite widespread opposition, the proposal may end up going into effect on account of political pressures the president is facing ahead of the midterm elections, now just six weeks away.
While Trump has long insisted higher fuel costs are a “small price to pay” for neutralizing Iran, most Americans don’t feel that way. Sixty-one percent of voters view prices at the pump as a significant concern, according to a September Fox News poll. And a number of GOP lawmakers have recently expressed that something must be done.
“What has overpowered cooler heads [in the White House] is the absolutely, sky-is-falling, we-have-to-do-something concern about prices at the pump” contingent, an oil industry executive told Politico. “That camp has been swept aside by the political camp, which says, ‘dammit, something has to happen.’”
The 80-year-old president is disposed to believe any backlash to the 90-day ban could be thought of as “a December problem,” the source said.
“This is not true,” a White House spokesperson told The Independent. “Politico published this Fake News even though the Energy Secretary publicly addressed this earlier today.”
The spokesperson pointed to comments from Wright delivered at the United Nations General Assembly, where he said the administration would not fully ban diesel exports, but instead implement restrictions.

articles.title_orig: Meta's Muse AI Agent Sees Fastest Adoption Since ChatGPT. Time to Buy Meta Stock?
articles.title_zh: Meta's Muse AI Agent Sees Fastest Adoption Since ChatGPT. Time to Buy Meta Stock?
articles.content_orig:
The rise in the utility of artificial intelligence (AI) in recent years has been nothing short of breathtaking. The buzz surrounding generative AI has given way to AI agents capable of multi-step reasoning. This allows them to complete complex tasks by breaking them down into smaller steps while keeping their digital eye on the ultimate goal. Big tech companies have been deploying AI agents to streamline processes, write code, simplify digital advertising, and more. Now, AI agents have made the leap to the consumer realm.
Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 15x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »
Earlier this month, Meta Platforms (NASDAQ:META) unveiled Muse, which the company describes as "the world's first personal AI agent." The company noted that the agent, powered by its Muse Spark Frontier model, doesn't just answer questions. Muse could be used "right out of the box" -- without any specialized training or background -- to send emails, plan and book travel, or make online purchases.
Just weeks later, the Muse AI agent has gone viral, outpacing the adoption of ChatGPT at its launch, and it shows no signs of slowing.
Image source: The Motley Fool.
Meta's Muse is experiencing the fastest adoption since the dawn of ChatGPT in Nov. 2022. In the first 12 days after its release, Muse recorded 1.8 million iOS mobile downloads from the Apple App Store in the U.S. and Canada, according to market intelligence platform Apptopia. That compares with 1.3 million downloads for ChatGPT in its first 12 days after release. Including activity from Alphabet's Android App Store, total Muse downloads reach 2.8 million.
That was enough to vault Muse to the No. 1 spot among the most-downloaded free iOS apps, pushing ChatGPT to No. 2. Muse has maintained an iOS rating of 4.9 out of 5 stars, with more than 36,000 reviews (as of this writing). It has since become the most downloaded free Android app.
The AI agent is also generating strong engagement. Muse had 642,000 daily active users in its first 12 days post-launch, compared to 231,000 for ChatGPT during the same period post-release. Meta is leveraging its vast social media user base of more than 3.6 billion to cross-promote Muse. Apptopia reported that 95% of Muse adopters were also Facebook users, while 63% were Instagram users.
A host of high-profile partnerships
Muse isn't only seeing rapid adoption by consumers, but businesses are lining up to integrate the AI agent into their digital retail and fintech platforms:
Shopify announced plans to integrate Muse into its e-commerce platform, allowing the agent to browse products and facilitate purchases via Shop Pay from its merchant stores on behalf of users.
Digital payments specialist PayPal is partnering with Meta to integrate Muse into its global merchant network, helping users find products and use PayPal's secure checkout to complete the transaction.
Online travel agent Expedia announced it was joining Muse to help users plan trips and make travel arrangements.
Fintech platform Stripe was a Muse launch partner, announcing that it would integrate its Link digital wallet with Muse, allowing users to pay for agentic purchases. The system provides a one-time-use card number so the user's actual data remains hidden.
Maplebear, the parent of Instacart, announced that its grocery delivery system will integrate directly with Muse to help simplify shopping.
Some of these collaborations have only been announced this week, so as Muse adoption continues to gain ground, expect new partnerships to crop up.
One of the persistent questions among Meta investors is how the company would generate revenue from its heavy AI spending. The rapid adoption of Muse helps answer that question. In addition to its free, limited-use tier, Muse has paid monthly tiers of $20 and $100.
If just 1% of Meta's 3.6 billion users were to subscribe to the $20 tier -- a conservative assumption given its early reception -- the company could generate more than $8.6 billion in incremental revenue annually. If Muse catches on, the stakes could be even higher.
The combination of increasing consumer adoption and the growing number of enterprise partners signals that Muse could join the ranks of the most popular AI apps -- which would be extremely lucrative for Meta and its shareholders.
Despite the intriguing opportunity, the stock is selling for a surprisingly affordable 28 times earnings -- even after its recent rally. That's why Meta is a buy.
